SFLCompat/Recall/Check.lean

1-module
2-
3--- For testing cases in this file
4-meta import all Init.Prelude
5-public meta import SFLCompat.Recall.Common
6-
7-/-!
8-# Recall, checked by elaboration
9-
10-`sf_recall` lets a chapter restate a definition from earlier in the
11-development while the build checks that the restatement means the same
12-thing. The restated declaration is elaborated for real, inside a hidden
13-namespace, and compared with the original up to definitional equality; the
14-temporary declaration is then rolled back.
15-
16-Two forms:
17-
18-```
19-sf_recall
20-  def twice (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) : Nat := f <| f n
21-
22-sf_recall statement twice_id : twice id 3 = 3
23-```
24-
25-What is compared:
26-
27-* types, always;
28-* a `def`'s value, safety, and abbreviation status;
29-* an inductive's constructors, one by one (names, parameter and index
30-  counts, and each constructor's type);
31-* a structure's fields, field defaults, and type-class registration;
32-* a theorem's statement, never its proof.
33-
34-So a recalled definition may be reformatted or rephrased into something
35-definitionally equal, and a theorem may be reproved differently or, with
36-the `statement` form, restated without any proof. The command is global and
37-available wherever this module is imported.
38--/
39-
40-
41-namespace SFLCompat.Recall.Check
42-
43-open Lean Elab Command Meta
44-
45-meta section
46-
47-structure DeclId where
48-  /-- This could be a private name. -/
49-  actual : Name
50-  display : Name
51-
52-def DeclId.ofActual (actual : Name) : DeclId :=
53-  { actual, display := privateToUserName actual }
54-
55-/-- Look up the actual name in temp elaboration namespace -/
56-def tempDeclId (userName : Name) : CommandElabM DeclId := do
57-  let env ← getEnv
58-  let privateName := mkPrivateName env userName
59-  let actual ←
60-    if env.contains privateName then pure privateName
61-    else if env.contains userName then pure userName
62-    else throwError "the re-elaborated declaration '{userName}' was not found"
63-  return .ofActual actual
64-
65-def renameBackName (chk orig n : Name) : Name :=
66-  if chk.isPrefixOf n then n.replacePrefix chk orig
67-  else
68-    let chk := privateToUserName chk
69-    if chk.isPrefixOf n then n.replacePrefix chk orig else n
70-
71-/--
72-Replaces the name prefix `chk` with `orig` in every constant that `e`
73-mentions: `chk` itself becomes `orig`, and a longer name such as a hidden
74-constructor `chk.mk` becomes `orig.mk`. Constructor types mention the
75-hidden inductive type's name in argument and resulting positions, so this
76-rewrite is what makes a re-elaborated declaration comparable with the
77-original.
78--/
79-def renameBack (chk orig : DeclId) (e : Expr) : Expr :=
80-  e.replace fun
81-    | .const n us =>
82-      let n' := renameBackName chk.actual orig.actual n
83-      if n == n' then none else some (.const n' us)
84-    | _ => none
85-
86-/--
87-Applies `renameBack` to the expressions recorded in an info tree. The info
88-recorded while elaborating the hidden copy mentions the hidden constants,
89-so hovers over a recalled declaration would otherwise display the hidden
90-names; rewriting before the trees are stored makes them display the
91-originals, which also exist after the hidden copy is rolled back.
92--/
93-partial def renameBackInfoTree (chk orig : DeclId) (t : InfoTree) : InfoTree :=
94-  match t with
95-  | .context (.parentDeclCtx n) t' =>
96-    .context (.parentDeclCtx (renameBackName chk.actual orig.actual n))
97-      (renameBackInfoTree chk orig t')
98-  | .context ctx t' => .context ctx (renameBackInfoTree chk orig t')
99-  | .node i children =>
100-    let i := match i with
101-      | .ofTermInfo ti => .ofTermInfo (reTerm ti)
102-      | .ofDelabTermInfo dti => .ofDelabTermInfo { dti with toTermInfo := reTerm dti.toTermInfo }
103-      | other => other
104-    .node i (children.map (renameBackInfoTree chk orig))
105-  | .hole m => .hole m
106-where
107-  reTerm (ti : TermInfo) : TermInfo :=
108-    { ti with
109-      expr := renameBack chk orig ti.expr
110-      expectedType? := ti.expectedType?.map (renameBack chk orig) }
111-
112-/-- A specialization of universe parameters to a declaration.
113-  It stores level parameters of a `ConstantInfo` and mvars created from these parameters.
114--/
115-abbrev Specialization := List Name × List Level
116-
117-def renameBackS (specialization? : Option Specialization)
118-    (chk orig : DeclId) (e : Expr) : Expr :=
119-  match specialization? with
120-  | none => renameBack chk orig e
121-  | some (_params, levels) =>
122-    e.replace fun
123-      | .const n _ =>
124-        let n' := renameBackName chk.actual orig.actual n
125-        if n == n' then none else some <| .const n' levels
126-      | _ => none
127-
128-def levelsFor (specialization : Specialization) (info : ConstantInfo) :
129-    TermElabM (List Level) :=
130-  let (params, levels) := specialization
131-  info.levelParams.mapM fun param =>
132-    match params.findIdx? (· == param) with
133-    | some index => pure levels[index]!
134-    | none => throwError
135-      "universe parameter '{param}' of '{info.name}' is not a parameter of the recalled declaration"
136-
137-/--
138-Checks that the types of the original constant `x` and its re-elaborated
139-counterpart `chk` agree, definitionally. The restated type is first
140-rewritten by `renameBack renChk renOrig`; the defaults compare a
141-declaration against its own hidden copy, and the constructor check
142-overrides them with the enclosing inductive types, whose names the
143-constructor types mention. The restatement's universe parameters are
144-instantiated with the original's.
145--/
146-def checkTypesMatch (x chk : DeclId) (ref : Syntax)
147-    (specialization? : Option Specialization)
148-    (renChk : DeclId := chk) (renOrig : DeclId := x) (hint : MessageData := .nil) :
149-    TermElabM Unit := do
150-  let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
151-  let chkInfo ← getConstInfo chk.actual
152-  if specialization?.isNone then
153-    -- no specialization, do strict check first
154-    unless origInfo.levelParams.length == chkInfo.levelParams.length do
155-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"universe parameters of '{x.display}' do not match" ++ hint)
156-  let origType ← match specialization? with
157-    | none => pure origInfo.type
158-    | some s => origInfo.instantiateTypeLevelParams <$> levelsFor s origInfo
159-  let chkType := match specialization? with
160-    | none => (renameBackS specialization? renChk renOrig chkInfo.type).instantiateLevelParams
161-        chkInfo.levelParams (origInfo.levelParams.map .param)
162-    | some _ => renameBackS specialization? renChk renOrig chkInfo.type
163-  unless ← isDefEq chkType origType do
164-    throwErrorAt ref
165-      (m!"the statement of '{x.display}' does not match.\n\
166-          Original:{indentD origInfo.type}\nRestated:{indentD chkType}" ++ hint)
167-
168-/--
169-All constructor syntax nodes of a command, in source order: an inductive
170-type's `| name : ...` alternatives and a structure's `name ::` header.
171--/
172-partial def ctorStxs (stx : Syntax) : Array Syntax :=
173-  let inner := stx.getArgs.flatMap ctorStxs
174-  if stx.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.ctor
175-      || stx.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.structCtor then
176-    #[stx] ++ inner
177-  else inner
178-
179-/-- Does the syntax contain a doc comment? -/
180-def hasDocComment (stx : Syntax) : Bool :=
181-  (stx.find? (·.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.docComment)).isSome
182-
183-/--
184-Suggestions localized to a mismatched constructor, returned as a pair of
185-hints for name errors and for type errors. An inductive type's `| name : ...` alternative is replaced
186-with the original constructor's own source. A structure's `name ::` header
187-can carry a name fix but not a field fix, so its type errors keep `outer`,
188-the suggestion that replaces the whole restatement. A constructor without
189-syntax also falls back to `outer`.
190--/
191-def ctorHints (ctorRef : Syntax) (origCtor origShort : Name) (outer : MessageData) :
192-    TermElabM (MessageData × MessageData) := do
193-  try
194-    if ctorRef.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.ctor then
195-      let origSrc := dedent (← sourceOf origCtor)
196-      -- A restatement without a doc comment gets a suggestion without one;
197-      -- the meaning check does not compare documentation.
198-      let origSrc := if hasDocComment ctorRef then origSrc
199-        else stripLeadingComments origSrc
200-      let restatedSrc ← sourceOfSyntax ctorRef
201-      let h ← replaceWithOriginalHint ctorRef origSrc restatedSrc
202-      return (h, h)
203-    if ctorRef.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.structCtor then
204-      let restatedSrc ← sourceOfSyntax ctorRef
205-      let h ← replaceWithOriginalHint ctorRef s!"{origShort} ::" restatedSrc
206-      return (h, outer)
207-    return (outer, outer)
208-  catch _ => return (outer, outer)
209-
210-/--
211-Checks a re-elaborated declaration against the original, definitionally.
212-Errors point at `ref`, the restated command, except for constructor
213-mismatches, which point at the offending constructor within it.
214--/
215-def checkMatchCore (x chk : DeclId) (ref : Syntax)
216-    (specialization? : Option (List Name × List Level))
217-    (hint : MessageData := .nil) : TermElabM Unit := do
218-  checkTypesMatch x chk ref specialization? (hint := hint)
219-  let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
220-  let chkInfo ← getConstInfo chk.actual
221-  match origInfo, chkInfo with
222-  | .defnInfo orig, .defnInfo restated =>
223-    let origVal ← match specialization? with
224-      | none => pure orig.value
225-      | some s => origInfo.instantiateValueLevelParams! <$> levelsFor s origInfo
226-    let chkVal := match specialization? with
227-      | none => (renameBackS specialization? chk x restated.value).instantiateLevelParams
228-          restated.levelParams (orig.levelParams.map .param)
229-      | some _ => renameBackS specialization? chk x restated.value
230-    unless ← isDefEq chkVal origVal do
231-      throwErrorAt ref
232-        (m!"the value of '{x.display}' does not match.\n\
233-            Original:{indentD orig.value}\nRestated:{indentD chkVal}" ++ hint)
234-  | .inductInfo orig, .inductInfo restated =>
235-    unless orig.numParams == restated.numParams && orig.numIndices == restated.numIndices do
236-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"parameters or indices of '{x.display}' do not match" ++ hint)
237-    unless orig.ctors.length == restated.ctors.length do
238-      throwErrorAt ref
239-        (m!"'{x.display}' has {orig.ctors.length} constructors, \
240-            the restatement has {restated.ctors.length}" ++ hint)
241-    -- A `structure` that writes no `name ::` header has a constructor
242-    -- without syntax; the whole command remains the fallback position.
243-    let ctorRefs := ctorStxs ref
244-    let mut i := 0
245-    for origCtorActual in orig.ctors, chkCtorActual in restated.ctors do
246-      let origCtor := DeclId.ofActual origCtorActual
247-      let chkCtor := DeclId.ofActual chkCtorActual
248-      let ctorRef := ctorRefs[i]?.getD ref
249-      let origShort := origCtor.actual.replacePrefix x.actual .anonymous
250-      let (nameHint, typeHint) ← ctorHints ctorRef origCtor.actual origShort hint
251-      let renamedChkCtor := DeclId.ofActual <|
252-        chkCtor.actual.replacePrefix chk.actual x.actual
253-      unless origCtor.actual == renamedChkCtor.actual do
254-        throwErrorAt ctorRef
255-          (m!"constructor '{renamedChkCtor.display}' does not match \
256-              '{origCtor.display}'" ++ nameHint)
257-      checkTypesMatch origCtor chkCtor ctorRef specialization?
258-        (renChk := chk) (renOrig := x) (hint := typeHint)
259-      i := i + 1
260-    -- A structure's field names are part of its interface, and the
261-    -- constructor's type does not record them, so they are compared
262-    -- through the environment's structure information.
263-    let env ← getEnv
264-    match getStructureInfo? env x.actual, getStructureInfo? env chk.actual with
265-    | some origSi, some chkSi =>
266-      let origFields := origSi.fieldNames.map DeclId.ofActual
267-      let chkFields := chkSi.fieldNames.map DeclId.ofActual
268-      unless origFields.map (·.actual) == chkFields.map (·.actual) do
269-        throwErrorAt ref
270-          (m!"the fields of '{x.display}' do not match.\n\
271-              Original:{indentD (toMessageData (origFields.map (·.display)).toList)}\n\
272-              Restated:{indentD (toMessageData (chkFields.map (·.display)).toList)}" ++ hint)
273-      unless getOutParamPositions? env x.actual == getOutParamPositions? env chk.actual
274-          && getOutLevelParamPositions? env x.actual == getOutLevelParamPositions? env chk.actual do
275-        throwErrorAt ref (m!"the type-class metadata of '{x.display}' does not match" ++ hint)
276-    | some _, none =>
277-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"'{x.display}' is a structure, but the restatement is not" ++ hint)
278-    | none, some _ =>
279-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"'{x.display}' is not a structure, but the restatement is one" ++ hint)
280-    | none, none => pure ()
281-  -- A theorem's proof is not compared; restating it as a `def` is also
282-  -- accepted, since only the statement matters.
283-  | .thmInfo _, .thmInfo _ => pure ()
284-  | .thmInfo _, .defnInfo _ => pure ()
285-  | .axiomInfo _, .axiomInfo _ => pure ()
286-  | .opaqueInfo _, .opaqueInfo _ => pure ()
287-  | _, _ =>
288-    throwErrorAt ref
289-      (m!"'{x.display}' and its restatement are different kinds of declaration" ++ hint)
290-
291-/--
292-Run `checkpointDefEq` in `TermElabM`.
293-Note: this is only for universe level constraints solving in `isDefEq` and
294-has nothing to do with the elaborator.
295--/
296-def checkpointDefEq' (action : TermElabM Bool) : TermElabM Bool :=
297-  controlAt MetaM fun runInBase =>
298-    checkpointDefEq (mayPostpone := false) (runInBase action)
299-
300-def checkMatch (x chk : DeclId) (ref : Syntax)
301-    (strictUniverse : Bool) (hint : MessageData := .nil) : TermElabM Unit := do
302-  let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
303-  let chkInfo ← getConstInfo chk.actual
304-  if origInfo.levelParams.length == chkInfo.levelParams.length then
305-    -- if the definition being to check has exactly the same number of the parameters,
306-    -- treat it as no specialization in checking
307-    checkMatchCore x chk ref none hint
308-  else if !strictUniverse && !origInfo.levelParams.isEmpty && chkInfo.levelParams.isEmpty then
309-    -- if all parameters have been specified (monomorphic), do check with specialization
310-    let succeeded ← checkpointDefEq' do
311-      let levels ← mkFreshLevelMVarsFor origInfo
312-      checkMatchCore x chk ref (some (origInfo.levelParams, levels)) hint
313-      pure true
314-    unless succeeded do
315-      throwErrorAt ref (m!"the statement of '{x.display}' does not match" ++ hint)
316-  else
317-    throwErrorAt ref (m!"universe parameters of '{x.display}' do not match" ++ hint)
318-
319-
320-/--
321-`sf_recall` restates a definition from earlier in the development and checks
322-that the restatement means the same thing. `sf_recall statement x : T` checks
323-that `T` matches the statement of the theorem `x`.
324--/
325-syntax (name := recallChk) "sf_recall " command : command
326-
327-@[inherit_doc recallChk]
328-syntax (name := recallChkStrict) "sf_recall" " +" noWs &"strictUniverse" ppSpace command : command
329-
330-@[inherit_doc recallChk]
331-syntax (name := recallChkStmt) "sf_recall " &"statement " ident " : " term : command
332-
333-
334-def elabRecallCommand (cmd : Syntax) (strictUniverse : Bool) : CommandElabM Unit := do
335-  let decl ← declaredName cmd
336-  let xActual ← liftCoreM <| withoutExporting <|
337-    realizeGlobalConstNoOverloadWithInfo decl.ident
338-  let x := DeclId.ofActual xActual
339-  -- The restatement elaborates unchanged inside a fresh hidden namespace:
340-  -- self-references (an inductive's own name in its constructor types, in
341-  -- resulting-type position included) resolve to the hidden copy, and
342-  -- every other name resolves as it would at the recall site. The
343-  -- namespace comes from the name generator: `_uniq` names cannot be
344-  -- written in source, so it is collision-free, and unlike a macro-scoped
345-  -- name it is an ordinary component, so declarations under it keep the
346-  -- prefix structure that `renameBack` and the constructor comparison
347-  -- rely on.
348-  let ns ← liftCoreM (mkFreshId : CoreM Name)
349-  -- Any mismatch gets a clickable fix: replace the restatement with the
350-  -- original's source text, indented like the restatement. The helpers
351-  -- for recovering and re-indenting source are shared with the
352-  -- byte-for-byte variant.
353-  -- A failed hint must not fail the check: not every constant has a
354-  -- declaration range or sources on the search path.
355-  let hint ←
356-    try
357-      let original := dedent (← sourceOf x.actual)
358-      let original := if hasDocComment cmd then original
359-        else stripLeadingComments original
360-      let restated ← sourceOfSyntax cmd
361-      liftCoreM <| replaceWithOriginalHint cmd original restated
362-    catch _ => pure .nil
363-  let envBefore ← getEnv
364-  try
365-    let chk ← withScope (fun sc => { sc with currNamespace := sc.currNamespace ++ ns }) do
366-      let saved ← getResetInfoTrees
367-      try
368-        elabCommand cmd
369-        -- this could be a private name
370-        let userName := (← getScope).currNamespace ++ decl.written
371-        let chk ← tempDeclId userName
372-        let inner ← getResetInfoTrees
373-        modifyInfoState fun s => { s with trees := saved ++ inner.map (renameBackInfoTree chk x) }
374-        return chk
375-      catch e =>
376-        let inner ← getResetInfoTrees
377-        modifyInfoState fun s => { s with trees := saved ++ inner }
378-        throw e
379-    runTermElabM fun _ => checkMatch x chk cmd strictUniverse (hint := hint)
380-  finally
381-    setEnv envBefore
382-
383-def elabRecallStatement (ident stmt : Syntax) : CommandElabM Unit := do
384-  let xActual ← liftCoreM <| withoutExporting <|
385-    realizeGlobalConstNoOverloadWithInfo ident
386-  let x := DeclId.ofActual xActual
387-  addConstInfo ident x.actual
388-  let region := mkNullNode #[ident, stmt]
389-  let restated ← sourceOfSyntax region
390-  runTermElabM fun _ => do
391-    -- The suggestion restates the original's type as the pretty-printer
392-    -- renders it. The statement cannot be carved out of the original's
393-    -- source, since finding its boundary would require parsing the
394-    -- source in the elaboration context of its declaration site.
395-    let hint ←
396-      try
397-        let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
398-        let printed ← ppExpr origInfo.type
399-        replaceWithOriginalHint region
400-          s!"{ident.getId} : {printed}" restated
401-      catch _ => pure .nil
402-    let t ← Term.elabType stmt
403-    Term.synthesizeSyntheticMVarsNoPostponing
404-    let t ← instantiateMVars (← Term.levelMVarToParam t)
405-    let origInfo ← getConstInfo x.actual
406-    let stParams := (collectLevelParams {} t).params
407-    unless stParams.size == origInfo.levelParams.length do
408-      throwErrorAt stmt (m!"universe parameters of '{x.display}' do not match" ++ hint)
409-    let t := t.instantiateLevelParams stParams.toList
410-      (origInfo.levelParams.map .param)
411-    unless ← isDefEq t origInfo.type do
412-      throwErrorAt stmt
413-        (m!"the restated statement of '{x.display}' does not match.\n\
414-            Original:{indentD origInfo.type}\nRestated:{indentD t}" ++ hint)
415-
416-
417-elab_rules : command
418-  | `(sf_recall $cmd:command) => elabRecallCommand cmd false
419-  | `(sf_recall +strictUniverse $cmd:command) => elabRecallCommand cmd true
420-  | `(sf_recall statement $ident:ident : $stmt:term) => elabRecallStatement ident stmt
421-
422-end
423-namespace Tests
424-
425-sf_recall
426-  inductive Nat where
427-  | zero
428-  | succ (n : Nat) : Nat
429-
430--- A constructor mismatch is reported at the offending constructor, not at
431--- the whole restatement.
432-/--
433-@ +4:2...26
434-error: the statement of 'Nat.succ' does not match.
435-Original:
436-  Nat → Nat
437-Restated:
438-  Nat → Nat → Nat
439-
440-Hint: Replace the restatement with the original:
441-  | succ (̲n̲ ̲: N̲a̲t̲)̲ ̲:̲ ̲Nat ̵→̵ ̵N̵a̵t̵ ̵→̵ ̵N̵a̵t̵
442--/
443-#guard_msgs (positions := true) in
444-sf_recall
445-  inductive Nat where
446-  | zero
447-  | succ : Nat → Nat → Nat
448-
449-inductive Palette where
450-  | red | green | blue
451-

SFLCompat/Recall/Common.lean

1-module
2-
3-public meta import Lean.Elab.Command
4-
5-namespace SFLCompat.Recall
6-
7-open Lean Elab Command
8-public meta section
9-
10-/-- All `declId` nodes in a command, in source order. -/
11-partial def declIds (stx : Syntax) : Array Syntax :=
12-  let inner := stx.getArgs.flatMap declIds
13-  if stx.isOfKind ``Lean.Parser.Command.declId then #[stx] ++ inner else inner
14-
15-/-- The syntax and written name of the single declaration in a recall command. -/
16-structure DeclSyntax where
17-  ident : Syntax
18-  written : Name
19-
20-/--
21-The `declId` node of a declaration command, together with the name written
22-in it. A command that declares several names (a `mutual` block) or none (an
23-anonymous `instance`, an `example`) is rejected.
24--/
25-def declaredName (cmd : Syntax) : CommandElabM DeclSyntax := do
26-  let defined := declIds cmd
27-  match h : defined.size with
28-  | 0 => throwErrorAt cmd "the restated command does not declare a name"
29-  | 1 =>
30-    let declId := defined[0]
31-    return { ident := declId[0], written := declId[0].getId }
32-  | n + 2 =>
33-    for h : i in 0...(n + 1) do
34-      logErrorAt defined[i]
35-        "the restated command declares several names; recall one declaration at a time"
36-    throwErrorAt defined[n + 1]
37-      "the restated command declares several names; recall one declaration at a time"
38-
39-/--
40-Removes the block indentation of a declaration's source text. The first
41-line starts at the declaration's first token and has no indentation of its
42-own; each following line is stripped of the smallest indentation found
43-among the non-blank ones. Restatements of the same text at different block
44-depths dedent to identical strings, and every other difference survives
45-dedenting.
46--/
47-def dedent (s : String) : String :=
48-  match indentWidth s, s.splitOn "\n" with
49-  | some n, first :: rest =>
50-    "\n".intercalate (first :: rest.map (fun l => String.ofList (l.toList.drop n)))
51-  | _, _ => s
52-where
53-  /-- The smallest indentation among the non-blank continuation lines. -/
54-  indentWidth (s : String) : Option Nat :=
55-    s.splitOn "\n" |>.drop 1 |>.map (·.toList)
56-      |>.filter (fun l => !l.all (·.isWhitespace))
57-      |>.map (fun l => (l.takeWhile (· == ' ')).length)
58-      |>.min?
59-
60-/--
61-Indents the continuation lines of dedented source text by `n` spaces, so
62-that the text reads correctly at the block depth of a restatement.
63--/
64-def reindent (s : String) (n : Nat) : String :=
65-  match s.splitOn "\n" with
66-  | [] => s
67-  | first :: rest =>
68-    let pad := String.ofList (List.replicate n ' ')
69-    "\n".intercalate (first :: rest.map fun l =>
70-      if l.toList.all (·.isWhitespace) then l else pad ++ l)
71-
72-/--
73-Removes the comments from the front of dedented source text, together with
74-the whitespace around them, so that a suggestion offered for a restatement
75-that carries no comments does not introduce any. The text of a declaration
76-or of a constructor begins with its doc comment when it has one, possibly
77-accompanied by ordinary comments, and a leading block comment ends at its
78-depth-balanced closing delimiter, so a character scan recognizes the
79-leading run of comments exactly. A comment elsewhere in the text cannot be
80-recognized without lexing and is left in place.
81--/
82-def stripLeadingComments (s : String) : String := Id.run do
83-  let mut cs := s.toList.dropWhile (·.isWhitespace)
84-  repeat
85-    if cs.take 2 == ['/', '-'] then
86-      cs := cs.drop 2
87-      let mut depth := 1
88-      while depth > 0 do
89-        match cs with
90-        | [] => return s
91-        | '/' :: '-' :: rest => depth := depth + 1; cs := rest
92-        | '-' :: '/' :: rest => depth := depth - 1; cs := rest
93-        | _ :: rest => cs := rest
94-    else if cs.take 2 == ['-', '-'] then
95-      cs := cs.dropWhile (· != '\n')
96-    else
97-      break
98-    cs := cs.dropWhile (·.isWhitespace)
99-  return String.ofList cs
100-
101-/--
102-A clickable suggestion that replaces the restated text at `span` with
103-`original`, which must already be dedented. The original's indentation is
104-moved to match the restatement's: the restatement's own indentation width
105-when it has continuation lines, one step past the span's start column when
106-it does not.
107--/
108-def replaceWithOriginalHint [Monad m] [MonadFileMap m] [MonadLiftT CoreM m]
109-    (span : Syntax) (original restated : String) : m MessageData := do
110-  let fileMap ← getFileMap
111-  let k := match dedent.indentWidth restated, span.getRange? with
112-    | some k, _ => k
113-    | none, some r => (fileMap.toPosition r.start).column + 2
114-    | none, none => 2
115-  MessageData.hint m!"Replace the restatement with the original:"
116-    #[{ suggestion := .string (reindent original k), span? := some span }]
117-
118-/--
119-The source text of the declaration of `x`, from the file that declared it.
120-
121-The location comes from the declaration range that Lean records for every
122-constant. A declaration from the current file is read out of the file map;
123-one from an imported module is read from its source file, found on the
124-source search path. In a book build the whole project's sources are on that
125-path, so definitions can be recalled across chapters.
126--/
127-def sourceOf [Monad m] [MonadEnv m] [MonadError m] [MonadFileMap m]
128-    [MonadLiftT IO m] [MonadLiftT BaseIO m] (x : Name) : m String := do
129-  let some ranges ← findDeclarationRanges? x
130-    | throwError "no declaration range recorded for '{x}'"
131-  let env ← getEnv
132-  let text ←
133-    match env.getModuleIdxFor? x with
134-    | none => pure (← getFileMap)
135-    | some idx => do
136-      let modName := env.allImportedModuleNames[idx.toNat]!
137-      let sp ← getSrcSearchPath
138-      let some path ← sp.findModuleWithExt "lean" modName
139-        | throwError "source for module '{modName}' is not on the search path"
140-      pure (FileMap.ofString (← IO.FS.readFile path))
141-  return String.Pos.Raw.extract text.source
142-    (text.ofPosition ranges.range.pos) (text.ofPosition ranges.range.endPos)
143-
144-/-- The source text of a piece of syntax in the current file. -/
145-def sourceOfSyntax [Monad m] [MonadError m] [MonadFileMap m]
146-    (stx : Syntax) : m String := do
147-  let some r := stx.getRange?
148-    | throwErrorAt stx "no source range"
149-  return String.Pos.Raw.extract (← getFileMap).source r.start r.stop
150-
151-end
152-
153-end SFLCompat.Recall

SFLCompat/Recall/Source.lean

1-module
2-
3-public meta import SFLCompat.Recall.Common
4-
5-/-!
6-# Recall, checked byte for byte
7-
8-`sf_recall_source` lets a chapter restate a definition from earlier in the
9-development while the build checks that the restatement matches the
10-original's source text, byte for byte. The restated text is what the
11-reader already saw, and it can never drift from the original.
12-
13-```
14-sf_recall_source
15-  def twice (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) : Nat := f (f n)
16-```
17-
18-The restated declaration is parsed but never elaborated; the check is
19-purely textual: after the block indentation is removed from each side, the
20-two texts must be equal, byte for byte. The restatement may sit at a
21-different indentation depth, but it may not be reflowed or respaced.
22-
23-The comparison covers whole declarations only. Carving a statement out of
24-the original's source would require parsing it, which is only possible in
25-the elaboration context of its declaration site; restating only a theorem
26-statement is therefore the province of `sf_recall statement`, which compares
27-elaborated types.
28--/
29-
30-namespace SFLCompat.Recall.Source
31-
32-open Lean Elab Command
33-
34-/--
35-`recall_source` restates a definition from earlier in the development and
36-checks that the restatement matches the original's source text, byte for
37-byte, modulo block indentation.
38--/
39-syntax (name := recallSrc) "sf_recall_source " command : command
40-
41-elab_rules : command
42-  | `(sf_recall_source $cmd:command) => do
43-    let decl ← declaredName cmd
44-    let x ← liftCoreM <| withoutExporting <|
45-      realizeGlobalConstNoOverloadWithInfo decl.ident
46-    -- The restatement is never elaborated, so it produces no info of its
47-    -- own. The whole compared region is one big reference to the original:
48-    -- hovering anywhere in it shows the original, and go-to-definition
49-    -- jumps to it.
50-    addConstInfo cmd x
51-    let restated ← sourceOfSyntax cmd
52-    let original ← sourceOf x
53-    unless dedent restated == dedent original do
54-      throwErrorAt cmd
55-        (m!"the restatement of '{privateToUserName x}' does not match its source.\n\
56-            Original:{indentD original}\nRestated:{indentD restated}"
57-          ++ (← liftCoreM <| replaceWithOriginalHint cmd (dedent original) restated))
58-
59-namespace Tests
60-
61-inductive Palette where
62-  | red | green | blue
63-
64-def twice (f : Nat → Nat) (n : Nat) : Nat := f (f n)
65-

1-import SFLCompat
2-
3---  # Slang: Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
4-
5---  ## Arithmetic and Boolean Expressions
6-
7---  ### Syntax
8-
9-namespace Slang
10-
11---  Abstract syntax trees for arithmetic and boolean
12---  expressions:
13-
14-inductive Aexp where
15-  | num (n : Nat)
16-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
17-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
18-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
19-
20-inductive Bexp where
21-  | bool (b : Bool)
22-  | eq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
23-  | neq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
24-  | le (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
25-  | gt (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
26-  | not (b : Bexp)
27-  | and (b₁ b₂ : Bexp)
28-
29---  ### Evaluation
30-
31---  *Evaluating* an arithmetic expression produces a number.
32-
33-namespace Aexp
34-def eval (a : Aexp) : Nat :=
35-  match a with
36-  | num   n     =>  n
37-  | plus  a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval + a₂.eval
38-  | minus a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval - a₂.eval
39-  | mult  a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval * a₂.eval
40-
41-@[simp] theorem eval_num (n : Nat) : (num n).eval = n := rfl
42-@[simp] theorem eval_plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (plus a₁ a₂).eval = a₁.eval + a₂.eval := rfl
43-@[simp] theorem eval_minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (minus a₁ a₂).eval = a₁.eval - a₂.eval := rfl
44-@[simp] theorem eval_mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (mult a₁ a₂).eval = a₁.eval * a₂.eval := rfl
45-
46-example : eval (.plus (.num 2) (.num 2)) = 4 := by simp
47-end Aexp
48-
49---  Similarly, evaluating a boolean expression yields a
50---  boolean.
51-
52-namespace Bexp
53-def eval (b : Bexp) : Bool :=
54-  match b with
55-  | bool b     =>  b
56-  | eq   a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval == a₂.eval
57-  | neq  a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval != a₂.eval
58-  | le   a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval ≤ a₂.eval
59-  | gt   a₁ a₂ =>  a₁.eval > a₂.eval
60-  | not  b₁    =>  !eval b₁
61-  | and  b₁ b₂ =>  eval b₁ && eval b₂
62-
63-@[simp] theorem eval_bool (b : Bool) : (bool b).eval = b := rfl
64-@[simp] theorem eval_eq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (eq a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval == a₂.eval) := rfl
65-@[simp] theorem eval_neq (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (neq a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval != a₂.eval) := rfl
66-@[simp] theorem eval_le (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (le a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval ≤ a₂.eval : Bool) := rfl
67-@[simp] theorem eval_gt (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) : (gt a₁ a₂).eval = (a₁.eval > a₂.eval : Bool) := rfl
68-@[simp] theorem eval_not (b : Bexp) : (not b).eval = !b.eval := rfl
69-@[simp] theorem eval_and (b₁ b₂ : Bexp) : (and b₁ b₂).eval = (b₁.eval && b₂.eval) := rfl
70-end Bexp
71-
72---  It's worth noting that `≤` and `>` are `Prop`-valued,
73---  i.e. `a₁.eval st ≤ a₂.eval st` is a proposition, but
74---  `Bexp.eval` returns a `Bool`, so Lean implicitly inserts
75---  a `decide` coercion. You can observe the call to
76---  `decide` by hovering over `Bexp.eval_le` and
77---  `Bexp.eval_gt`.
78-
79---  _Quiz:_
80-
81---  What does the following expression evaluate to?
82-
83---  Aexp.eval (.plus (.num 3) (.minus (.num 4) (.num 1)))
84-
85---  (A) true (B) false (C) 0 (D) 3 (E) 6
86-
87---  ### Optimization
88-
89-namespace Aexp
90-
91-def optimize0plus (a : Aexp) : Aexp :=
92-  match a with
93-  | num   n          => num n
94-  | plus  (num 0) e₂ => optimize0plus e₂
95-  | plus  e₁      e₂ => plus  (optimize0plus e₁) (optimize0plus e₂)
96-  | minus e₁      e₂ => minus (optimize0plus e₁) (optimize0plus e₂)
97-  | mult  e₁      e₂ => mult  (optimize0plus e₁) (optimize0plus e₂)
98-
99-example :
100-    Aexp.optimize0plus (.plus (.num 2)
101-                               (.plus (.num 0)
102-                                      (.plus (.num 0) (.num 1))))
103-      = .plus (.num 2) (.num 1) := by rfl
104-
105-theorem optimize0plus_sound (a : Aexp) :
106-    a.optimize0plus.eval = a.eval := by
107-  induction a with
108-  | num n => rfl
109-  | plus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
110-    cases a₁ with
111-    | num n =>
112-      cases n with
113-      | zero =>
114-        simp only [optimize0plus, eval_plus, eval_num, Nat.zero_add]
115-        exact ih₂
116-      | succ n =>
117-        simp only [optimize0plus, eval_plus, eval_num]
118-        rw [ih₂]
119-    | plus b₁ b₂ =>
120-      simp only [optimize0plus, eval_plus] at ih₁ ⊢
121-      rw [ih₁, ih₂]
122-    | minus b₁ b₂ =>
123-      simp only [optimize0plus, eval_plus] at ih₁ ⊢
124-      rw [ih₁, ih₂]
125-    | mult b₁ b₂ =>
126-      simp only [optimize0plus, eval_plus] at ih₁ ⊢
127-      rw [ih₁, ih₂]
128-  | minus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
129-    simp only [optimize0plus, eval_minus]
130-    rw [ih₁, ih₂]
131-  | mult a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
132-    simp only [optimize0plus, eval_mult]
133-    rw [ih₁, ih₂]
134-
135---  We can use `fun_induction` to achieve a much shorter
136---  proof.
137-
138-theorem optimize0plus_sound' (a : Aexp) :
139-    a.optimize0plus.eval = a.eval := by
140-  fun_induction Aexp.optimize0plus a <;> simp_all
141-
142-end Aexp
143-
144---  ### Exercise (3 stars): optimize0plus_sound ⭐⭐⭐
145-
146---  Since the `Aexp.optimize0plus` transformation doesn't
147---  change the value of an `Aexp`, we should be able to
148---  apply it to all the `Aexp`s that appear in a `Bexp`
149---  without changing the `Bexp`'s value. Write a function
150---  that performs this transformation on `Bexp`s and prove
151---  it sound. Use the combinators we've just seen to make
152---  the proof as short and elegant as possible.
153-
154-def Bexp.optimize0plus (b : Bexp) : Bexp := sorry
155-
156-theorem Bexp.optimize0plus_test1 :
157-    Bexp.optimize0plus
158-        (.not (.gt (.plus (.num 0) (.num 4)) (.num 8)))
159-      = (.not (.gt (.num 4) (.num 8))) := sorry
160-
161-theorem Bexp.optimize0plus_test2 :
162-    Bexp.optimize0plus
163-        (.and (.le (.plus (.num 0) (.num 4)) (.num 5)) (.bool true))
164-      = (.and (.le (.num 4) (.num 5)) (.bool true)) := sorry
165-
166-theorem Bexp.optimize0plus_sound (b : Bexp) :
167-    b.optimize0plus.eval = b.eval := by
168-  sorry
169-
170---  ### Exercise (4 stars): optimize (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐⭐
171-
172---  The optimization implemented by our `Aexp.optimize0plus`
173---  is only one of many possible optimizations on arithmetic
174---  and boolean expressions. Write a more sophisticated
175---  optimizer and prove it correct. (You will probably find
176---  it easiest to start small -- add just a single, simple
177---  optimization and its correctness proof -- and build up
178---  incrementally to something more interesting.)
179-
180---  ## Evaluation as a Relation
181-
182-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
183-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
184-  | plus {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
185-      EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
186-  | minus {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
187-      EvalR (.minus a₁ a₂) (n₁ - n₂)
188-  | mult {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
189-      EvalR (.mult a₁ a₂) (n₁ * n₂)
190-
191---  One comment on the style of this definition. We could
192---  instead have presented this relation with **positional**
193---  hypotheses -- no names for the premises.
194-
195-namespace ArithUnnamed
196-
197-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
198-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
199-  | plus {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} : EvalR a₁ n₁ → EvalR a₂ n₂ → EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
200-  | minus {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} : EvalR a₁ n₁ → EvalR a₂ n₂ → EvalR (.minus a₁ a₂) (n₁ - n₂)
201-  | mult {a₁ a₂ : Aexp} {n₁ n₂ : Nat} : EvalR a₁ n₁ → EvalR a₂ n₂ → EvalR (.mult a₁ a₂) (n₁ * n₂)
202-
203-end ArithUnnamed
204-
205---  It will be convenient to have an infix notation for
206---  `Aexp.EvalR`. We'll write `e ⇓ n` to mean that
207---  arithmetic expression `e` evaluates to value `n`. The
208---  `⇓` symbol is typed `\Downarrow`.
209-
210-namespace Aexp
211-scoped notation:55 e:56 " ⇓ " n:56 => EvalR e n
212-
213---  ### Inference Rule Notation
214-
215---  _Quiz:_
216-
217---  Which rules are needed to prove the following?
218-
219---  .mult (.plus (.num 3) (.num 1)) (.num 0) ⇓ 0
220-
221---  (A) `num` and `plus` (B) `num` only (C) `num` and `mult`
222---  (D) `mult` and `plus` (E) `num`, `mult`, and `plus`
223-
224---  ### Exercise (1 star): beval_rules (Optional, manually graded) ⭐
225-
226---  Here, again, is the definition of the `Bexp.eval`
227---  function:
228-
229---    def Bexp.eval (b : Bexp) : Bool :=
230---      match b with
231---      | bool b     => b
232---      | eq   a₁ a₂ => a₁.eval == a₂.eval
233---      | neq  a₁ a₂ => a₁.eval != a₂.eval
234---      | le   a₁ a₂ => a₁.eval ≤ a₂.eval
235---      | gt   a₁ a₂ => a₁.eval > a₂.eval
236---      | not  b₁    => !eval b₁
237---      | and  b₁ b₂ => eval b₁ && eval b₂
238-
239---  Write out a corresponding definition of boolean
240---  evaluation as a relation in inference rule notation.
241-
242---  ### Equivalence of the Definitions
243-
244---  It is straightforward to prove that the relational and
245---  functional definitions of evaluation agree.
246-
247-theorem evalR_iff_eval (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
248-    a ⇓ n ↔ a.eval = n := by
249-  constructor
250-  · intro h
251-    induction h with
252-    | num n => rfl
253-    | plus h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ => simp only [eval_plus]; rw [ih₁, ih₂]
254-    | minus h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ => simp only [eval_minus]; rw [ih₁, ih₂]
255-    | mult h₁ h₂ ih₁ ih₂ => simp only [eval_mult]; rw [ih₁, ih₂]
256-  · intro h
257-    subst h
258-    induction a with
259-    | num n => exact .num n
260-    | plus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ => exact .plus ih₁ ih₂
261-    | minus a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ => exact .minus ih₁ ih₂
262-    | mult a₁ a₂ ih₁ ih₂ => exact .mult ih₁ ih₂
263-
264---  We can make the proof quite a bit shorter using more
265---  automation like we did in the previous section.
266-
267-theorem evalR_iff_eval' (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
268-    a ⇓ n ↔ a.eval = n := by
269-  sorry
270-
271-end Aexp
272-
273---  ### Exercise (3 stars): bevalR ⭐⭐⭐
274-
275---  Write a relation `Bexp.EvalR` in the same style as
276---  `Aexp.EvalR`, and prove that it is equivalent to
277---  `Bexp.eval`.
278-
279-namespace Bexp
280-open scoped Aexp -- opens the ⇓ notation for Aexp.EvalR
281-
282-inductive EvalR : Bexp → Bool → Prop where
283-  -- FILL IN HERE
284-
285-scoped notation:55 e:56 " ⇓ " b:56 => EvalR e b
286-
287-theorem evalR_iff_eval (b : Bexp) (bv : Bool) :
288-    b ⇓ bv ↔ b.eval = bv := by
289-  sorry
290-
291-end Bexp
292-end Slang
293-
294---  ### Computational vs. Relational Definitions
295-
296---  Sometimes relational definitions are the only reasonable
297---  option...
298-
299-namespace Slang.AevalRDivision
300-
301---  For example, suppose that we wanted to extend the
302---  arithmetic operations with division:
303-
304-inductive Aexp where
305-  | num (n : Nat)
306-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
307-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
308-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
309-  | div (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)             -- NEW
310-
311---  Extending the definition of `Aexp.eval` to handle this
312---  new operation would not be straightforward due to
313---  division being a *partial* operation; i.e., what should
314---  we return as the result of `.div (.num 5) (.num 0)`? One
315---  option would be to lift the definition of `Aexp.eval` to
316---  return an option:
317-
318-namespace Aexp
319-
320-def eval (a : Aexp) : Option Nat :=
321-  match a with
322-  | num   n     =>  some n
323-  | plus  a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
324-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => some (n₁ + n₂)
325-                    | _, _ => none
326-  | minus a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
327-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => some (n₁ - n₂)
328-                    | _, _ => none
329-  | mult  a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
330-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => some (n₁ * n₂)
331-                    | _, _ => none
332-  | div   a₁ a₂ =>  match a₁.eval, a₂.eval with
333-                    | _, some 0 => none
334-                    | some n₁, some n₂ => if n₂ ∣ n₁ then some (n₁ / n₂) else none
335-                    | _, _ => none
336-end Aexp
337-
338---  This definition is a lot wordier than the earlier
339---  version. There are tools to reduce this overhead, namely
340---  monads, but we will not discuss these in Software
341---  Foundations in Lean. Curious readers can learn more
342---  about them from [Functional Programming in
343---  Lean](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/Monads/).
344-
345---  By contrast, partiality is no problem for the relational
346---  version of the definition.
347-
348---  What should `Aexp.eval` return for
349---  `.div (.num 1) (.num 0)`??
350-
351-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
352-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
353-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
354-      EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
355-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
356-      EvalR (.minus a₁ a₂) (n₁ - n₂)
357-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
358-      EvalR (.mult a₁ a₂) (n₁ * n₂)
359-  | div (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ n₃ : Nat)             -- NEW
360-      (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) (hpos : n₂ > 0) (hdiv : n₂ * n₃ = n₁) :
361-      EvalR (.div a₁ a₂) n₃
362-
363---  Notice that there are some inputs (those with a divisor
364---  of 0) for which this relation does not specify an
365---  output.
366-
367-end Slang.AevalRDivision
368-
369-namespace Slang.AevalRExtended
370-
371---  Another example: a *nondeterministic* number generator:
372-
373---  As another example, suppose that we want to extend the
374---  arithmetic operations by a nondeterministic number
375---  generator `any` that, when evaluated, may yield any
376---  number. (This is not the same as making a
377---  *probabilistic* choice among all numbers -- we only say
378---  which results are *possible*.)
379-
380-inductive Aexp where
381-  | any                            -- NEW
382-  | num (n : Nat)
383-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
384-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
385-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp)
386-
387---  Again, extending `Aexp.eval` would be tricky, since
388---  evaluation is now *not* a deterministic function from
389---  expressions to numbers; but extending the relation is no
390---  problem.
391-
392---  What should `Aexp.eval` do with nondeterminism??
393-
394-inductive Aexp.EvalR : Aexp → Nat → Prop where
395-  | any (n : Nat) : EvalR .any n                   -- NEW
396-  | num (n : Nat) : EvalR (.num n) n
397-  | plus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
398-      EvalR (.plus a₁ a₂) (n₁ + n₂)
399-  | minus (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
400-      EvalR (.minus a₁ a₂) (n₁ - n₂)
401-  | mult (a₁ a₂ : Aexp) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : EvalR a₁ n₁) (h₂ : EvalR a₂ n₂) :
402-      EvalR (.mult a₁ a₂) (n₁ * n₂)
403-
404-end Slang.AevalRExtended

407---  both, proved equivalent.

TS/Smallstep.lean

1-import TS.Slang
2-
3-import SFLCompat
4-
5---  # Smallstep: Small-step Operational Semantics
6-
7---  ## Big-step and Small-step Evaluation
8-
9---  Our semantics for expressions is written in the
10---  so-called "big-step" style. Evaluation rules take an
11---  expression to a final answer "all in one step":
12-
13---  2 + 2 + 3 * 4 ⇓ 16
14-
15---  But big-step semantics makes it hard to talk about what
16---  happens *along the way*.
17-
18---  *Small-step* style: alternatively, we can show how to
19---  "reduce" an expression to a simpler form by performing a
20---  single step of computation:
21-
22---  2 + 2 + 3 * 4
23---  ⟶ 2 + 2 + 12
24---  ⟶ 4 + 12
25---  ⟶ 16
26-
27---  Advantages of the small-step style include:
28-
29---  - Finer-grained "abstract machine", closer to real
30---    implementations.
31-
32---  - Extends smoothly to concurrent languages and languages
33---    with other sorts of *computational effects*.
34-
35---  - Separates *divergence* (nontermination) from
36---    *stuckness* (run-time error).
37-
38---  ## A Toy Language
39-
40-inductive Tm where
41-  | c (n : Nat)          -- Constant
42-  | p (t₁ t₂ : Tm)       -- Plus
43-
44---  A standard big-step evaluator, as a function.
45-
46-def evalF (t : Tm) : Nat :=
47-  match t with
48-  | .c n => n
49-  | .p t₁ t₂ => evalF t₁ + evalF t₂
50-
51---  Here is the same evaluator, written in exactly the same
52---  style, but formulated as an inductively defined
53---  relation. We use the notation `t ⇓ n` for "`t` evaluates
54---  to `n`."
55-
56---  The `notation` command below is how that is declared: it
57---  introduces `⇓` as infix syntax for the `Eval` relation
58---  defined with it, with a precedence saying how tightly it
59---  binds. This is the lightweight way to name a relation;
60---  later chapters, where a whole object language needs a
61---  grammar rather than a single operator, reach for
62---  `declare_syntax_cat` instead.
63-
64---  -------                (const)
65---                          c n ⇓ n
66-
67---                          t₁ ⇓ n₁
68---                          t₂ ⇓ n₂
69---                      -----------------          (plus)
70---                      p t₁ t₂ ⇓ n₁ + n₂
71-
72-inductive Eval : Tm → Nat → Prop where
73-  | const (n : Nat) : Eval (.c n) n
74-  | plus (t₁ t₂ : Tm) (n₁ n₂ : Nat) (h₁ : Eval t₁ n₁) (h₂ : Eval t₂ n₂) : Eval (.p t₁ t₂) (n₁ + n₂)
75-
76-notation:50 t " ⇓ " n => Eval t n
77-
78-namespace SimpleArith1
79-
80-inductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
81-  | plus (n₁ n₂ : Nat) :
82-      Step (.p (.c n₁) (.c n₂)) (.c (n₁ + n₂))
83-  | plusLeft (t₁ t₁' t₂ : Tm)
84-      (h : Step t₁ t₁') :
85-      Step (.p t₁ t₂) (.p t₁' t₂)
86-  | plusRight (n₁ : Nat) (t₂ t₂' : Tm)
87-      (h : Step t₂ t₂') :
88-      Step (.p (.c n₁) t₂) (.p (.c n₁) t₂')
89-
90-scoped notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Step t t'
91-
92---  Notice: each step reduces the *leftmost* `p` node that
93---  is ready to go — the first rule tells how to rewrite it,
94---  the second and third tell where to find it — and
95---  constants do not step to anything.
96-
97---  Let's pause and check a couple of examples of reasoning
98---  with the step relation.
99-
100---  If `t₁` steps to `t₁'`, then `p t₁ t₂` steps to
101---  `p t₁' t₂`.
102-
103-example :
104-    (.p
105-      (.p (.c 1) (.c 3))
106-      (.p (.c 2) (.c 4))) ⟶
107-    (.p
108-      (.c 4)
109-      (.p (.c 2) (.c 4))) := by
110-  apply Step.plusLeft; apply Step.plus
111-
112---  ### Exercise (1 star): test_step_2 ⭐
113-
114---  Right-hand sides step only once the left side is a
115---  value.
116-
117-example :
118-    (.p
119-      (.c 0)
120-      (.p
121-        (.c 2)
122-        (.p
123-          (.c 1)
124-          (.c 3))))
125-      ⟶
126-    (.p
127-      (.c 0)
128-      (.p
129-        (.c 2)
130-        (.c 4))) := by
131-  sorry
132-
133---  _Quiz:_
134-
135---  To what does the following term step?
136-
137---  .p
138---    (.p
139---      (.c 1)
140---      (.c 2))
141---    (.p
142---      (.c 1)
143---      (.c 2))
144-
145---  (A) `.c 6` (B) `.p (.c 3) (.p (.c 1) (.c 2))` (C)
146---  `.p (.p (.c 1) (.c 2)) (.c 3)` (D) `.p (.c 3) (.c 3)`
147---  (E) None of the above
148-
149---  _Quiz:_
150-
151---  What about this one?
152-
153---  .c 1
154-
155---  (A) `.c 1` (B) `.p (.c 0) (.c 1)` (C) None of the above
156-
157-end SimpleArith1
158-
159---  ## Relations
160-
161---  The step relation `⟶` is an example of a relation on
162---  `Tm`.
163-
164-def Relation (X : Type) := X → X → Prop
165-
166---  One simple property a relation may have is being
167---  *deterministic*: like Slang's big-step evaluation, each
168---  element is related to at most one other.
169-
170---  *Theorem*: For each `t`, there is at most one `t'` such
171---  that `t` steps to `t'`. We prove it by induction on the
172---  derivation of the first step.
173-
174---  *Proof sketch*: We show that if `x` steps to both `y₁`
175---  and `y₂`, then `y₁` and `y₂` are equal, by induction on
176---  a derivation of `x ⟶ y₁`. There are several cases,
177---  depending on the last rule used in this derivation and
178---  the last rule in the given derivation of `x ⟶ y₂`.
179-
180---  - If both are `plus`, the result is immediate.
181-
182---  - The cases when both derivations end with `plusLeft` or
183---    `plusRight` follow by the induction hypothesis.
184-
185---  - It cannot happen that one is `plus` and the other is
186---    `plusLeft`/`plusRight`, since this would imply that
187---    `x` has the form `p t₁ t₂` where both `t₁` and `t₂`
188---    are constants (by `plus`) *and* one of `t₁` or `t₂`
189---    has the form `p _`.
190-
191---  - Similarly, it cannot happen that one is `plusLeft` and
192---    the other is `plusRight`, since this would imply that
193---    `x` has the form `p t₁ t₂` where `t₁` has both the
194---    form `p t₁₁ t₁₂` and the form `c n`.
195-
196---  Formally,
197-
198-def Deterministic {X : Type} (R : Relation X) : Prop :=
199-  ∀ x y₁ y₂ : X, R x y₁ → R x y₂ → y₁ = y₂
200-
201-namespace SimpleArith2
202-
203-theorem step_deterministic : Deterministic SimpleArith1.Step := by
204-  intro x y₁ y₂ h₁
205-  induction h₁ generalizing y₂ with
206-  | plus n₁ n₂ =>
207-      intro h₂
208-      cases h₂ <;> first | rfl | cases ‹SimpleArith1.Step (.c _) _›
209-  | plusLeft t₁ t₁' t₂ hs ih =>
210-      intro h₂
211-      cases h₂ <;> first | cases ‹SimpleArith1.Step (.c _) _› | rw [ih _ ‹SimpleArith1.Step t₁ _›]
212-  | plusRight n₁ t₂ t₂' hs ih =>
213-      intro h₂
214-      cases h₂ <;> first | cases ‹SimpleArith1.Step (.c _) _› | rw [ih _ ‹SimpleArith1.Step t₂ _›]
215-
216-end SimpleArith2
217-
218---  ### Values
219-
220---  Final states of our machine are terms of the form `c n`.
221---  We call such terms *values*.
222-
223-inductive IsValue : Tm → Prop where
224-  | const (n : Nat) : IsValue (.c n)
225-
226---  Here are the formal rules.
227-
228-inductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
229-  | plus (n₁ n₂ : Nat) :
230-      Step (.p (.c n₁) (.c n₂)) (.c (n₁ + n₂))
231-  | plusLeft (t₁ t₁' t₂ : Tm)
232-      (h : Step t₁ t₁') :
233-      Step (.p t₁ t₂) (.p t₁' t₂)
234-  | plusRight (v₁ t₂ t₂' : Tm)
235-      (hv : IsValue v₁)
236-      (h : Step t₂ t₂') :
237-      Step (.p v₁ t₂) (.p v₁ t₂')
238-
239-notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Step t t'
240-
241---  ### Exercise (3 stars): redo_determinism ⭐⭐⭐
242-
243---  As a sanity check on this change, let's re-verify
244---  determinism. Here's an informal proof:
245-
246---  *Proof sketch*: We must show that if `x` steps to both
247---  `y₁` and `y₂`, then `y₁` and `y₂` are equal. Consider
248---  the final rules used in the derivations of `x ⟶ y₁` and
249---  `x ⟶ y₂`.
250-
251---  - If both are `plus`, the result is immediate.
252-
253---  - The cases when both derivations end with `plusLeft` or
254---    `plusRight` follow by the induction hypothesis.
255-
256---  - It cannot happen that one is `plus` and the other is
257---    `plusLeft`/`plusRight`, since this would imply that
258---    `x` has the form `p t₁ t₂` where both `t₁` and `t₂`
259---    are constants (by `plus`) *and* one of `t₁` or `t₂`
260---    has the form `p _`.
261-
262---  - Similarly, it cannot happen that one is `plusLeft` and
263---    the other is `plusRight`, since this would imply that
264---    `x` has the form `p t₁ t₂` where `t₁` both has the
265---    form `p t₁₁ t₁₂` and is a value (hence has the form
266---    `c n`).
267-
268---  Most of this proof is the same as the one above. But to
269---  get maximum benefit from the exercise you should try to
270---  write your formal version from scratch and just use the
271---  earlier one if you get stuck. The impossible cross-cases
272---  now also use the fact that a `IsValue` (a `c n`) cannot
273---  step.
274-
275-theorem step_deterministic : Deterministic Step := by
276-  sorry
277-
278---  ### Strong Progress and Normal Forms
279-
280-theorem strong_progress (t : Tm) : IsValue t ∨ ∃ t', t ⟶ t' := by
281-  induction t with
282-  | c n => left; exact .const n
283-  | p t₁ t₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
284-      right
285-      cases ih₁ with
286-      | inl hv₁ =>
287-          cases ih₂ with
288-          | inl hv₂ =>
289-              cases hv₁ with
290-              | const n₁ =>
291-                  cases hv₂ with
292-                  | const n₂ => exact ⟨.c (n₁ + n₂), .plus n₁ n₂⟩
293-          | inr h₂ =>
294-              obtain ⟨t₂', ht₂⟩ := h₂
295-              exact ⟨.p t₁ t₂', .plusRight t₁ t₂ t₂' hv₁ ht₂⟩
296-      | inr h₁ =>
297-          obtain ⟨t₁', ht₁⟩ := h₁
298-          exact ⟨.p t₁' t₂, .plusLeft t₁ t₁' t₂ ht₁⟩
299-
300-def IsNormalForm {X : Type} (R : Relation X) (t : X) : Prop :=
301-  ¬ ∃ t', R t t'
302-
303---  We can use this terminology to generalize the
304---  observation we made in the strong progress theorem: in
305---  this language (though not necessarily, in general),
306---  normal forms and values are actually the same thing.
307-
308-theorem value_is_nf (v : Tm) (h : IsValue v) : IsNormalForm Step v := by
309-  intro hc
310-  obtain ⟨t', ht⟩ := hc
311-  cases h with
312-  | const n => cases ht
313-
314-theorem nf_is_value (t : Tm) (h : IsNormalForm Step t) : IsValue t := by
315-  cases strong_progress t with
316-  | inl hv => exact hv
317-  | inr hstep => exact absurd hstep h
318-
319-theorem nf_same_as_value (t : Tm) : IsNormalForm Step t ↔ IsValue t :=
320-  ⟨nf_is_value t, value_is_nf t⟩
321-
322---  Why is this interesting? Because `IsValue` is a
323---  *syntactic* concept — it is defined by looking at the
324---  way a term is written — while `IsNormalForm` is a
325---  *semantic* one — it is defined by looking at how the
326---  term steps.
327-
328---  It is not obvious that these concepts should
329---  characterize the same set of terms!
330-
331---  Indeed, we could easily have written the definitions
332---  (incorrectly) so that they would *not* coincide.
333-
334---  Suppose, for example, we define `IsValue` so that it
335---  includes some terms that are not finished reducing.
336---  (Even if you don't work the exercise
337---  `value_not_same_as_normal_form1` below and the following
338---  ones, make sure you can think of an example of such a
339---  term.)
340-
341-namespace Temp1
342-
343-inductive IsValue : Tm → Prop where
344-  | const (n : Nat) : IsValue (.c n)
345-  | funny (t₁ : Tm) (n : Nat) : IsValue (.p t₁ (.c n))     -- <---
346-
347-inductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
348-  | plus (n₁ n₂ : Nat) : Step (.p (.c n₁) (.c n₂)) (.c (n₁ + n₂))
349-  | plusLeft (t₁ t₁' t₂ : Tm) (h : Step t₁ t₁') : Step (.p t₁ t₂) (.p t₁' t₂)
350-  | plusRight (v₁ t₂ t₂' : Tm) (hv : IsValue v₁) (h : Step t₂ t₂') : Step (.p v₁ t₂) (.p v₁ t₂')
351-

370-    ∃ v, IsValue v ∧ ¬ IsNormalForm Step v := by
371-  apply Exists.intro (.p (.c 0) (.c 0))
372-  apply And.intro (.funny _ 0)
373-  sorry

378-
379---  Or we might (again, wrongly) define `Step` so that it
380---  permits something designated as a value to reduce
381---  further. We again lose the property that values are the
382---  same as normal forms.

384-namespace Temp2

386-inductive IsValue : Tm → Prop where

388-
389-inductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
390-  | funny (n : Nat) : Step (.c n) (.p (.c n) (.c 0))     -- <--- NEW
391-  | plus (n₁ n₂ : Nat) : Step (.p (.c n₁) (.c n₂)) (.c (n₁ + n₂))
392-  | plusLeft (t₁ t₁' t₂ : Tm) (h : Step t₁ t₁') : Step (.p t₁ t₂) (.p t₁' t₂)
393-  | plusRight (v₁ t₂ t₂' : Tm) (hv : IsValue v₁) (h : Step t₂ t₂') : Step (.p v₁ t₂) (.p v₁ t₂')

403-    ∃ v, IsValue v ∧ ¬ IsNormalForm Step v := by
404-  apply Exists.intro (.c 5)

411-
412---  Finally, we might define `IsValue` and `Step` so that
413---  there is some term that is *not* a value but that *also*
414---  cannot take a step. Such terms are said to be *stuck*.
415---  In this case, this is caused by a mistake in the
416---  semantics, but we will also see situations where, even
417---  in a correct language definition, it makes sense to
418---  allow some terms to be stuck. (Note that `plusRight` is
419---  missing below.)

421-namespace Temp3
422-
423-inductive IsValue : Tm → Prop where
424-  | const (n : Nat) : IsValue (.c n)

428-  | plusLeft (t₁ t₁' t₂ : Tm) (h : Step t₁ t₁') : Step (.p t₁ t₂) (.p t₁' t₂)

438-    ∃ t, ¬ IsValue t ∧ IsNormalForm Step t := by
439-  apply Exists.intro (.p (.c 1) (.p (.c 1) (.c 2)))
440-  apply And.intro
441-  · sorry
442-  · sorry
443-
444-end Temp3

446---  ## Multi-Step Reduction
447-
448-inductive Multi {X : Type} (R : Relation X) : X → X → Prop where
449-  | refl (x : X) : Multi R x x
450-  | step (x y z : X) (h₁ : R x y) (h₂ : Multi R y z) : Multi R x z
451-
452---  We write `⟶*` for the `Multi Step` relation on terms
453-
454-notation:40 t:41 " ⟶* " t':41 => Multi Step t t'
455-
456---  The relation `Multi R` has several crucial properties.
457-
458-attribute [refl] Multi.refl
459-
460-example : (.c 5 : Tm) ⟶* .c 5 := by rfl
461-
462-example : (.p (.c 1) (.c 2)) ⟶* .c (1 + 2) := by
463-  apply Multi.step (y := .c (1 + 2))
464-  · exact .plus 1 2
465-  · rfl
466-
467-theorem multi_single {X : Type} (R : Relation X) (x y : X) (h : R x y) :
468-    Multi R x y :=
469-  .step x y y h (.refl y)
470-
471-theorem multi_trans {X : Type} (R : Relation X) (x y z : X)
472-    (g : Multi R x y) (h : Multi R y z) : Multi R x z := by
473-  induction g with
474-  | refl a => exact h
475-  | step a b c h₁ h₂ ih => exact .step a b z h₁ (ih h)
476-
477---  _Quiz:_
478-
479---  Which of the following relations on numbers *cannot* be
480---  expressed as `Multi R` for some `R`?
481-
482---  (A) less than or equal (B) strictly less than (C) equal
483---  (D) none of the above
484-
485---  ### Examples
486-
487-example :
488-    (.p (.p (.c 0) (.c 3)) (.p (.c 2) (.c 4))) ⟶* .c ((0 + 3) + (2 + 4)) := by
489-  apply Multi.step (y := .p (.c (0 + 3)) (.p (.c 2) (.c 4)))
490-  · exact .plusLeft _ _ _ (.plus 0 3)
491-  apply Multi.step (y := .p (.c (0 + 3)) (.c (2 + 4)))
492-  · exact .plusRight _ _ _ (.const _) (.plus 2 4)
493-  · exact multi_single _ _ _ (.plus (0 + 3) (2 + 4))
494-

572---  ### Equivalence of Big-Step and Small-Step
573-
574---  Having defined the operational semantics of our tiny
575---  programming language in two different ways (big-step and
576---  small-step), it makes sense to ask whether these
577---  definitions actually define the same thing!
578-
579---  They do, though it takes a little work to show it. The
580---  details are left as an exercise. We consider the two
581---  implications separately. First, big-step evaluation
582---  implies multi-step reduction to a value.
583-
584---  ### Exercise (3 stars): multistep_of_eval ⭐⭐⭐
585-
586-theorem multistep_of_eval (t : Tm) (n : Nat) (h : t ⇓ n) : t ⟶* .c n := by
587-  sorry
588-
589---  The key ideas in the proof can be seen in the following
590---  picture:
591-
592---  p t₁ t₂ ⟶            (by plusLeft)
593---  p t₁' t₂ ⟶           (by plusLeft)
594---  p t₁'' t₂ ⟶          (by plusLeft)
595---  ...
596---  p (c n₁) t₂ ⟶        (by plusRight)
597---  p (c n₁) t₂' ⟶       (by plusRight)
598---  p (c n₁) t₂'' ⟶      (by plusRight)
599---  ...
600---  p (c n₁) (c n₂) ⟶    (by plus)
601---  c (n₁ + n₂)
602-
603---  That is, the multi-step reduction of a term of the form
604---  `p t₁ t₂` proceeds in three phases:
605-
606---  - First, we use `plusLeft` some number of times to
607---    reduce `t₁` to a normal form, which must (by
608---    `nf_same_as_value`) be a term of the form `c n₁` for
609---    some `n₁`.
610-
611---  - Next, we use `plusRight` some number of times to
612---    reduce `t₂` to a normal form, which must again be a
613---    term of the form `c n₂` for some `n₂`.
614-
615---  - Finally, we use `plus` one time to reduce
616---    `p (c n₁) (c n₂)` to `c (n₁ + n₂)`.
617-
618---  To formalize this intuition, you'll need the congruence
619---  lemmas from above, plus some basic properties of `⟶*`
620---  (that it is reflexive, transitive, and includes `⟶`).
621-

623-

625---  `multistep_of_eval`. (A paper exercise — there is no
626---  Lean proof to fill in here.)
627-
628---  For the converse, we need one lemma, which establishes a
629---  relation between single-step reduction and big-step
630---  evaluation. A single step preserves the big-step value.
631-

757---  _Quiz:_
758-
759---  Which of these properties does this small-step semantics
760---  for `Slang` expressions satisfy? (Yes or No for each.)
761-
762---  - determinism
763-
764---  - strong progress (every non-value takes a step)
765-
766---  - values and normal forms coincide (i.e., there are no
767---    "stuck" terms)
768-
769---  - the step relation is normalizing (i.e., evaluation
770---    always terminates)

795-
796---  `⟶n`: like `⟶a`, but with the `IsAValue` guard on the

798---  evaluation order is nondeterministic.

801-  | plusLeft (a₁ a₁' a₂ : Aexp) (h : ANStep a₁ a₁') :  ANStep (.plus a₁ a₂) (.plus a₁' a₂)
802-  | plusRight (a₁ a₂ a₂' : Aexp) (h : ANStep a₂ a₂') : ANStep (.plus a₁ a₂) (.plus a₁ a₂')
803-  | plus (n₁ n₂ : Nat) : ANStep (.plus (.num n₁) (.num n₂)) (.num (n₁ + n₂))
804-  | minusLeft (a₁ a₁' a₂ : Aexp) (h : ANStep a₁ a₁') : ANStep (.minus a₁ a₂) (.minus a₁' a₂)
805-  | minusRight (a₁ a₂ a₂' : Aexp) (h : ANStep a₂ a₂') : ANStep (.minus a₁ a₂) (.minus a₁ a₂')
806-  | minus (n₁ n₂ : Nat) : ANStep (.minus (.num n₁) (.num n₂)) (.num (n₁ - n₂))
807-  | multLeft (a₁ a₁' a₂ : Aexp) (h : ANStep a₁ a₁') : ANStep (.mult a₁ a₂) (.mult a₁' a₂)
808-  | multRight (a₁ a₂ a₂' : Aexp) (h : ANStep a₂ a₂') : ANStep (.mult a₁ a₂) (.mult a₁ a₂')
809-  | mult (n₁ n₂ : Nat) : ANStep (.mult (.num n₁) (.num n₂)) (.num (n₁ * n₂))

879---  ### A Small-Step Stack Machine
880-
881---  Our last example is a small-step semantics for a *stack
882---  machine* that evaluates arithmetic expressions. The
883---  machine's instructions push a constant or combine the
884---  top two stack entries. The machine's behavior should
885---  match the big-step `Aexp.eval` function defined earlier.
886-
887---  A *program* is a list of instructions, and the *stack*
888---  is a list of numbers.
889-
890-inductive SInstr where
891-  | push (n : Nat)
892-  | plus
893-  | minus
894-  | mult
895-
896-abbrev Stack := List Nat
897-abbrev Prog := List SInstr
898-
899---  The compiler emits code in the postfix order sketched
900---  above:
901-
902-def compile : Aexp → Prog
903-  | .num n => [.push n]
904-  | .plus a₁ a₂ => compile a₁ ++ compile a₂ ++ [.plus]
905-  | .minus a₁ a₂ => compile a₁ ++ compile a₂ ++ [.minus]
906-  | .mult a₁ a₂ => compile a₁ ++ compile a₂ ++ [.mult]
907-
908-example : compile (.plus (.num 2) (.num 3)) = [.push 2, .push 3, .plus] := rfl
909-
910---  Now the small-step machine itself: each step consumes
911---  the next instruction and updates the stack.
912-
913-inductive StackStep : Prog × Stack → Prog × Stack → Prop where
914-  | push (p : Prog) (stk : Stack) (n : Nat) : StackStep (.push n :: p, stk) (p, n :: stk)
915-  | plus (p : Prog) (stk : Stack) (n m : Nat) :
916-      StackStep (.plus :: p, n :: m :: stk) (p, (m + n) :: stk)
917-  | minus (p : Prog) (stk : Stack) (n m : Nat) :
918-      StackStep (.minus :: p, n :: m :: stk) (p, (m - n) :: stk)
919-  | mult (p : Prog) (stk : Stack) (n m : Nat) :
920-      StackStep (.mult :: p, n :: m :: stk) (p, (m * n) :: stk)
921-
922---  The machine is deterministic:
923-
924-theorem stack_step_deterministic : Deterministic StackStep := by
925-  intro x y₁ y₂ h₁ h₂
926-  cases h₁ <;> cases h₂ <;> rfl
927-

938---  *any* stack `stk`. (Reassociating the `++`s with
939---  `List.append_assoc`, and chaining steps with
940---  `multi_trans`/`multi_single`, are the moves you need.)
941-
942-theorem compiler_is_correct (a : Aexp) :
943-    Multi StackStep (compile a, []) ([], [a.eval]) := by
944-  sorry
945-
946-end Slang
