TS/Stlc.lean

1-import Lean.PrettyPrinter.Delaborator
2-import Lean.PrettyPrinter.Parenthesizer
3-import LF.Typeclasses
4-import TS.Smallstep
5-
6-import SFLCompat
7-
8---  # Stlc: The Simply Typed Lambda-Calculus
9-
10---  Our job for this chapter: Formalize a small *functional*
11---  language and its type system.
12-
13---  Language: The *simply typed lambda-calculus* (STLC).
14-
15---  - A small subset of Lean's built-in functional
16---    language...
17-
18---  - ...but we'll use different concrete syntax (to avoid
19---    confusion, and for consistency with standard
20---    treatments)
21-
22---  Main new technical challenges:
23-
24---  - variable binding
25---  - substitution
26-
27---  The STLC lives in the lower-left front corner of the
28---  famous *lambda cube* (also called the *Barendregt
29---  Cube*), which visualizes three sets of features that can
30---  be added to its simple core:
31-
32---  Calculus of Constructions
33---   type operators +--------+
34---                 /|       /|
35---                / |      / |
36---  polymorphism +--------+  |
37---               |  |     |  |
38---               |  +-----|--+
39---               | /      | /
40---               |/       |/
41---               +--------+ dependent types
42---             STLC
43-
44---  Moving from bottom to top in the cube corresponds to
45---  adding *polymorphic types* like `∀ α : Type, α → α`.
46---  Adding *just* polymorphism gives us the famous
47---  Girard-Reynolds calculus, System F.
48-
49---  Moving from front to back corresponds to adding *type
50---  operators* like `List`.
51-
52---  Moving from left to right corresponds to adding
53---  *dependent types* like `∀ n, ArrayOfSize n`.
54-
55---  The top right corner on the back, which combines all
56---  three features, is called the *Calculus of
57---  Constructions*. First studied by Coquand and Huet, it
58---  forms the foundation of Lean's logic.
59-
60---  ## Overview
61-
62---  Begin with some set of *base types* (here, just `Bool`)
63-
64---  Add: variables, function abstractions, and applications
65-
66---  Informal concrete syntax of terms `t`:
67-
68---  t ::= x                     (variable)
69---      | λ x : T . t           (abstraction)
70---      | t t                   (application)
71---      | true                  (constant true)
72---      | false                 (constant false)
73---      | if t then t else t    (conditional)
74-
75---  The *types* of the STLC include the base type `Bool` for
76---  boolean values and arrow types for functions.
77-
78---  T ::= Bool
79---      | T → T
80-
81---  Some examples of STLC terms:
82-
83---  `λx:Bool. x`
84-
85---  The identity function for booleans.
86-
87---  `(λx:Bool. x) true`
88-
89---  The identity function for booleans, applied to the
90---  boolean `true`.
91-
92---  `λx:Bool. if x then false else true`
93-
94---  The boolean "not" function.
95-
96---  `λx:Bool. true`
97-
98---  The constant function that takes every (boolean)
99---  argument to `true`.
100-
101---  `λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x`
102-
103---  A two-argument function that takes two booleans and
104---  returns the first one.
105-
106---  `(λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x) false true`
107-
108---  A two-argument function that takes two booleans and
109---  returns the first one, applied to the booleans `false`
110---  and `true`.
111-
112---  `λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)`
113-
114---  A higher-order function that takes a *function* `f`
115---  (from booleans to booleans) as an argument, applies `f`
116---  to `true`, and applies `f` again to the result.
117-
118---  `(λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)) (λx:Bool. false)`
119-
120---  The same higher-order function, applied to the
121---  constantly `false` function.
122-
123---  Now reconsider our examples, each along with its type:
124-
125---  - `λx:Bool. x` has type `Bool → Bool`
126-
127---  - `(λx:Bool. x) true` has type `Bool`
128-
129---  - `λx:Bool. if x then false else true` has type
130---    `Bool → Bool`
131-
132---  - `λx:Bool. true` has type `Bool → Bool`
133-
134---  - `λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x` has type `Bool → Bool → Bool`
135---    (i.e., `Bool → (Bool → Bool)`)
136-
137---  - `(λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x) false true` has type `Bool`
138-
139---  The last two, higher-order examples are left off the
140---  list on purpose — working out their types is the subject
141---  of the quizzes that follow.
142-
143---  Note that *all* functions are anonymous.
144-
145---  We'll see how to add named function declarations as
146---  "syntactic sugar" in the `MoreStlc` chapter.
147-
148---  _Quiz:_
149-
150---  What is the type of the following term?
151-
152---    λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)
153-
154---  (A) `Bool → (Bool → Bool)`
155-
156---  (B) `(Bool → Bool) → Bool`
157-
158---  (C) `Bool → Bool`
159-
160---  (D) `Bool`
161-
162---  (E) none of the above
163-
164---  _Quiz:_
165-
166---  How about the type of this one?
167-
168---    (λf:Bool → Bool. f (f true)) (λx:Bool. false)
169-
170---  (A) `Bool → (Bool → Bool)`
171-
172---  (B) `(Bool → Bool) → Bool`
173-
174---  (C) `Bool → Bool`
175-
176---  (D) `Bool`
177-
178---  (E) none of the above
179-
180---  ## Syntax
181-
182---  We next formalize the syntax of the STLC.
183-
184-namespace Stlc
185-
186-open scoped MyGetElem
187-
188---  ### Types
189-
190-inductive Ty where
191-  | bool
192-  | arrow (T₁ T₂ : Ty)
193-
194---  ### Terms
195-
196-inductive Tm where
197-  | var (x : String)
198-  | app (t₁ t₂ : Tm)
199-  | abs (x : String) (T : Ty) (t : Tm)
200-  | tru
201-  | fls
202-  | ite (c t e : Tm)
203-
204---  We need some notation magic to set up the concrete
205---  syntax, as we did in the Types chapter...
206-
207---  Types and terms are both written inside `<{ … }>`; `~e`
208---  escapes to Lean.
209-
210---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: types)
211-
212---  The `stlcTy` grammar covers `Bool`, arrows (written `→`
213---  or `->`, associating to the right), parentheses, and
214---  `~e`. A bare identifier other than `Bool` is spliced in
215---  as a Lean term, so a local `T` — or any Lean expression
216---  of type `Ty` — can appear directly inside the brackets.
217-
218---  To extend the grammar, a later chapter adds a `syntax`
219---  line to the category and a matching `macro_rules` case;
220---  that is all it takes to add a new type construct.
221-
222-declare_syntax_cat stlcTy
223-syntax:max "~" term:max : stlcTy
224-syntax:max "(" stlcTy ")" : stlcTy
225-syntax:max ident : stlcTy
226-syntax:50 stlcTy:51 " → " stlcTy:50 : stlcTy
227-syntax:50 stlcTy:51 " -> " stlcTy:50 : stlcTy
228-syntax:max (name := tyBracket) "<{ " stlcTy " }>" : term
229-
230-macro_rules (kind := tyBracket)
231-  | `(<{ ~$T:term }>)    => pure T
232-  | `(<{ ($T:stlcTy) }>) => `(<{ $T:stlcTy }>)
233-  | `(<{ $x:ident }>) =>
234-      match x.getId.toString with
235-      | "Bool" => `(Ty.bool)
236-      | _ => `(($x : Ty))
237-  | `(<{ $T₁:stlcTy → $T₂:stlcTy }>)  => `(Ty.arrow <{ $T₁:stlcTy }> <{ $T₂:stlcTy }>)
238-  | `(<{ $T₁:stlcTy -> $T₂:stlcTy }>) => `(Ty.arrow <{ $T₁:stlcTy }> <{ $T₂:stlcTy }>)
239-
240---  END DETAILS
241-
242---  We'll write types inside of `<{ ... }>` brackets:
243-
244-#check <{ Bool }>
245-#check <{ Bool -> Bool }>
246-#check <{ (Bool -> Bool) -> Bool }>
247-
248---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: terms)
249-
250---  Terms are built from variables, application (associating
251---  to the left), abstraction, the two boolean constants,
252---  and conditionals. A binding occurrence — the `x` in
253---  `λ x : T . t` — has a small grammar of its own,
254---  `stlcVar`, and `varStr` turns it into the string that
255---  `Tm.abs` stores.
256-
257---  Because types and terms share the brackets, each
258---  `macro_rules` group says which bracket it belongs to
259---  (`kind := tyBracket`, `kind := tmBracket`), and each
260---  antiquote in a nested quotation says which grammar it
261---  came from. A bare identifier is the one genuinely
262---  overlapping case: `Bool` in term position would
263---  otherwise quietly become a variable named `Bool`, so
264---  that rule rejects it, which also settles which grammar a
265---  lone `<{ Bool }>` belongs to.
266-
267---  The last production, `[x := s] t`, is the notation for
268---  substitution; we give it its meaning when we define
269---  substitution below. It binds tighter than application,
270---  so `[x:=s] t₁ t₂` is the application of `[x:=s] t₁` to
271---  `t₂`, and a `λ` or `if` body must be parenthesized:
272---  `[x:=s] (λ y : Bool . x)`.
273-
274-declare_syntax_cat stlcVar
275-syntax:max ident : stlcVar
276-syntax:max "~" term:max : stlcVar
277-
278-open Lean in
279-/-- The string named by a variable in binding position. -/
280-def varStr (x : TSyntax `stlcVar) : MacroM Term :=
281-  match x with
282-  | `(stlcVar| $i:ident) => pure (quote i.getId.toString : Term)
283-  | `(stlcVar| ~$e)      => pure e
284-  | _ => Macro.throwUnsupported
285-
286-declare_syntax_cat stlcTm
287-syntax:max "~" term:max : stlcTm
288-syntax:max "(" stlcTm ")" : stlcTm
289-syntax:max ident : stlcTm
290-syntax:75 stlcTm:75 ppSpace stlcTm:76 : stlcTm
291-syntax:50 "λ " stlcVar " : " stlcTy " . " stlcTm:50 : stlcTm
292-syntax:50 "if " stlcTm:51 " then " stlcTm:50 " else " stlcTm:50 : stlcTm
293-syntax:max "[" stlcVar " := " stlcTm "] " stlcTm:max : stlcTm
294-syntax:max (name := tmBracket) "<{ " stlcTm " }>" : term
295-
296-open Lean in
297-macro_rules (kind := tmBracket)
298-  | `(<{ ~$e:term }>)    => pure e
299-  | `(<{ ($t:stlcTm) }>) => `(<{ $t:stlcTm }>)
300-  | `(<{ $x:ident }>) =>
301-      match x.getId.toString with
302-      | "true"  => `(Tm.tru)
303-      | "false" => `(Tm.fls)
304-      | "Bool"  => Macro.throwErrorAt x "`Bool` is a type, not a term"
305-      | _       => `(Tm.var $(quote x.getId.toString))
306-  | `(<{ $t₁:stlcTm $t₂:stlcTm }>) => `(Tm.app <{ $t₁:stlcTm }> <{ $t₂:stlcTm }>)
307-  | `(<{ λ $x : $T . $t }>) => do
308-      `(Tm.abs $(← varStr x) <{ $T:stlcTy }> <{ $t:stlcTm }>)
309-  | `(<{ if $c then $t else $e }>) =>
310-      `(Tm.ite <{ $c:stlcTm }> <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $e:stlcTm }>)
311-
312---  END DETAILS
313-
314---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: printing it back)
315-
316---  A *delaborator* runs the grammar backwards: it rebuilds
317---  the concrete syntax from a `Ty` or `Tm` value, so that
318---  types and terms appearing in goals and in `#check`
319---  output print as `<{ λ x : Bool . x }>` rather than as a
320---  pile of constructors. (Setting `pp.notation false` turns
321---  it off, revealing the underlying representation.)
322-
323-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Parenthesizer in
324-/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `stlcTy` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
325-@[category_parenthesizer stlcTy]
326-def stlcTy.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
327-  maybeParenthesize `stlcTy true wrapParens prec <|
328-    parenthesizeCategoryCore `stlcTy prec
329-where
330-  wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
331-    let pstx ← `(stlcTy| ($(⟨stx⟩)))
332-    return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
333-
334-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Parenthesizer in
335-/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `stlcTm` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
336-@[category_parenthesizer stlcTm]
337-def stlcTm.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
338-  maybeParenthesize `stlcTm true wrapParens prec <|
339-    parenthesizeCategoryCore `stlcTm prec
340-where
341-  wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
342-    let pstx ← `(stlcTm| ($(⟨stx⟩)))
343-    return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
344-
345-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
346-/-- Rebuild `stlcTy` concrete syntax from a `Ty` value. -/
347-partial def delabTyInner : DelabM (TSyntax `stlcTy) := do
348-  let stx ←
349-    match_expr ← getExpr with
350-    | Ty.bool => `(stlcTy| $(mkIdent `Bool):ident)
351-    | Ty.arrow _ _ => do
352-        let a ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTyInner
353-        let b ← withAppArg delabTyInner
354-        `(stlcTy| $a → $b)
355-    | _ => do
356-        match ← delab with
357-        | `($i:ident) => `(stlcTy| $i:ident)
358-        | e => `(stlcTy| ~$e)
359-  (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
360-
361-open Lean in
362-/-- Is `s` usable as a bare identifier in the object syntax? -/
363-def isPlainName (s : String) : Bool :=
364-  !s.isEmpty && s != "_" && !s.front.isDigit &&
365-    s.all fun c => c.isAlphanum || c == '_'
366-
367-open Lean in
368-/-- Is `s` usable as a bare variable in `stlcTm` rather than as reserved syntax? -/
369-def isPlainTmVarName (s : String) : Bool :=
370-  isPlainName s && s != "true" && s != "false" && s != "Bool"
371-
372-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
373-/-- Rebuild `stlcVar` concrete syntax from the string in a binding position. -/
374-def delabVarInner : DelabM (TSyntax `stlcVar) := do
375-  match ← delab with
376-  | `($s:str) =>
377-      if isPlainName s.getString then
378-        `(stlcVar| $(mkIdent (Name.mkSimple s.getString)):ident)
379-      else `(stlcVar| ~$s)
380-  | e => `(stlcVar| ~$e)
381-
382-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
383-/-- Rebuild `stlcTm` concrete syntax from a `Tm` value. -/
384-partial def delabTmInner : DelabM (TSyntax `stlcTm) := do
385-  let stx ←
386-    match_expr ← getExpr with
387-    | Tm.tru => `(stlcTm| $(mkIdent `true):ident)
388-    | Tm.fls => `(stlcTm| $(mkIdent `false):ident)
389-    | Tm.var _ => do
390-        let x ← withAppArg delab
391-        match x with
392-        | `($s:str) =>
393-            if isPlainTmVarName s.getString then
394-              `(stlcTm| $(mkIdent (Name.mkSimple s.getString)):ident)
395-            else
396-              let var : Term := mkIdent ``Stlc.Tm.var
397-              `(stlcTm| ~($var $x))
398-        | _ =>
399-            let var : Term := mkIdent ``Stlc.Tm.var
400-            `(stlcTm| ~($var $x))
401-    | Tm.app _ _ => do
402-        let f ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
403-        let a ← withAppArg delabTmInner
404-        `(stlcTm| $f $a)
405-    | Tm.abs _ _ _ => do
406-        let x ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabVarInner
407-        let T ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTyInner
408-        let t ← withAppArg delabTmInner
409-        `(stlcTm| λ $x : $T . $t)
410-    | Tm.ite _ _ _ => do
411-        let c ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
412-        let t ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
413-        let e ← withAppArg delabTmInner
414-        `(stlcTm| if $c then $t else $e)
415-    | _ => do
416-        -- `subst` is defined below, so it is matched by name rather than with
417-        -- `match_expr`; a substitution prints in its own bracket notation.
418-        let e ← getExpr
419-        if e.getAppFn.constName? == some `Stlc.subst && e.getAppNumArgs == 3 then
420-          let x ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabVarInner
421-          let s ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
422-          let t ← withAppArg delabTmInner
423-          `(stlcTm| [$x := $s] $t)
424-        else
425-          match ← delab with
426-          | `($i:ident) => `(stlcTm| $i:ident)
427-          | e => `(stlcTm| ~$e)
428-  (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
429-
430-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
431-@[delab app.Stlc.Ty.bool, delab app.Stlc.Ty.arrow]
432-def delabTy : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
433-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
434-    | Ty.bool => true | Ty.arrow _ _ => true | _ => false
435-  match ← delabTyInner with
436-  | `(stlcTy| ~$e) => pure e
437-  | e => `(<{ $e:stlcTy }>)
438-
439-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
440-@[delab app.Stlc.Tm.var, delab app.Stlc.Tm.app, delab app.Stlc.Tm.abs,
441-  delab app.Stlc.Tm.tru, delab app.Stlc.Tm.fls, delab app.Stlc.Tm.ite]
442-def delabTm : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
443-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
444-    | Tm.var _ => true | Tm.app _ _ => true | Tm.abs _ _ _ => true
445-    | Tm.tru => true | Tm.fls => true | Tm.ite _ _ _ => true
446-    | _ => false
447-  match ← delabTmInner with
448-  | `(stlcTm| ~($e)) => pure e
449-  | `(stlcTm| ~$e) => pure e
450-  | e => `(<{ $e:stlcTm }>)
451-
452---  END DETAILS
453-
454---  Here are the terms we will use as running examples,
455---  written in the new notation:
456-
457-abbrev idB := <{ λ x : Bool . x }>
458-
459-abbrev idBB := <{ λ x : Bool → Bool . x }>
460-
461-abbrev idBBBB := <{ λ x : (Bool → Bool) → (Bool → Bool) . x }>
462-
463-abbrev k := <{ λ x : Bool . λ y : Bool . x }>
464-
465-abbrev notB := <{ λ x : Bool . if x then false else true }>
466-
467---  Note that an abstraction `λ x : T . t` (formally,
468---  `Tm.abs` applied to `x`, `T`, and `t`) is always
469---  annotated with the type `T` of its parameter, in
470---  contrast to Lean (and other functional languages like
471---  ML, Haskell, etc.), which use type inference to fill in
472---  missing annotations. We're not considering type
473---  inference at all here.
474-
475---  ## Operational Semantics
476-
477---  To define the small-step semantics of STLC terms...
478-
479---  - We begin by defining the set of values.
480-
481---  - Next, we define *free variables* and *substitution*.
482---    These are used in the reduction rule for application
483---    expressions.
484-
485---  - Finally, we give the small-step relation itself.
486-
487---  ### Values
488-
489---  To define the values of the STLC, we have a few cases to
490---  consider.
491-
492---  First, for the boolean part of the language, the
493---  situation is clear: `true` and `false` are the only
494---  values. An `if` expression is never a value.
495-
496---  Second, an application is not a value: it represents a
497---  function being invoked on some argument, which clearly
498---  still has work left to do.
499-
500---  Third, for abstractions, we have a choice:
501-
502---  - We can say that `λx:T. t` is a value only when `t` is
503---    a value — i.e., only if the function's body has been
504---    reduced (as much as it can be without knowing what
505---    argument it is going to be applied to).
506-
507---  - Or we can say that `λx:T. t` is always a value, no
508---    matter whether `t` is one or not — in other words, we
509---    can say that reduction stops at abstractions.
510-
511---  Our usual way of evaluating expressions in Lean makes
512---  the first choice — for example,
513-
514-#reduce fun _x : Bool => 3 + 4
515-
516---  yields:
517-
518---    fun _x => 7
519-
520---  But Lean is rather unusual in this respect. Most
521---  functional programming languages make the second choice
522---  — reduction of a function's body only begins when the
523---  function is actually applied to an argument.
524-
525---  We also make the second choice here.
526-
527-inductive Tm.IsValue : Tm → Prop where
528-  | abs (x : String) (T₂ : Ty) (t₁ : Tm) : Tm.IsValue <{ λ ~x : ~T₂ . ~t₁ }>
529-  | tru : Tm.IsValue <{ true }>
530-  | fls : Tm.IsValue <{ false }>
531-
532-theorem idB_value : idB.IsValue := .abs ..
533-theorem idBB_value : idBB.IsValue := .abs ..
534-theorem notB_value : notB.IsValue := .abs ..
535-
536---  ### STLC Programs
537-
538---  Finally, we must consider what constitutes a *complete*
539---  program.
540-
541---  Intuitively, a "complete program" must not refer to any
542---  undefined variables. We'll see shortly how to define the
543---  *free* variables in a STLC term. A complete program,
544---  then, is one that is *closed* — that is, that contains
545---  no free variables.
546-
547---  (Conversely, a term that may contain free variables is
548---  often called an *open term*.)
549-
550---  Having made the choice not to reduce under abstractions,
551---  we don't need to worry about whether variables are
552---  values, since we'll always be reducing programs "from
553---  the outside in," and that means the `step` relation will
554---  always be working with closed terms.
555-
556---  ### Substitution
557-
558---  Now we come to the heart of the STLC: the operation of
559---  *substituting* one term for a variable in another term.
560---  This operation is used below to define the operational
561---  semantics of function application, where we will need to
562---  substitute the argument term for the function parameter
563---  in the function's body. For example, we reduce
564-
565---    (λx:Bool. if x then true else x) false
566-
567---  to
568-
569---    if false then true else false
570-
571---  by substituting `false` for the parameter `x` in the
572---  body of the function.
573-
574---  In general, we need to be able to substitute some given
575---  term `s` for occurrences of some variable `x` in another
576---  term `t`. Informally, this is written `[x:=s]t` and
577---  pronounced "substitute `s` for `x` in `t`."
578-
579---  Here are some examples:
580-
581---  - `[x:=true] (if x then true else false)` yields
582---    `if true then true else false`
583-
584---  - `[x:=true] x` yields `true`
585-
586---  - `[x:=true] (if x then x else y)` yields
587---    `if true then true else y`
588-
589---  - `[x:=true] y` yields `y`
590-
591---  - `[x:=true] false` yields `false` (vacuous
592---    substitution)
593-
594---  - `[x:=true] (λy:Bool. if y then x else false)` yields
595---    `λy:Bool. if y then true else false`
596-
597---  - `[x:=true] (λy:Bool. x)` yields `λy:Bool. true`
598-
599---  - `[x:=true] (λy:Bool. y)` yields `λy:Bool. y`
600-
601---  - `[x:=true] (λx:Bool. x)` yields `λx:Bool. x`
602-
603---  The last example is illuminating: substituting `x` with
604---  `true` in `λx:Bool. x` does *not* yield `λx:Bool. true`!
605---  The reason for this is that the `x` in the body of
606---  `λx:Bool. x` is *bound* by the abstraction: it is a new,
607---  local name that just happens to be spelled the same as
608---  some global name `x`.
609-
610---  Here is the definition, informally...
611-
612---    [x:=s]x               = s
613---    [x:=s]y               = y                     if x ≠ y
614---    [x:=s](λx:T. t)       = λx:T. t
615---    [x:=s](λy:T. t)       = λy:T. [x:=s]t         if x ≠ y
616---    [x:=s](t₁ t₂)         = ([x:=s]t₁) ([x:=s]t₂)
617---    [x:=s]true            = true
618---    [x:=s]false           = false
619---    [x:=s](if t₁ then t₂ else t₃) =
620---                    if [x:=s]t₁ then [x:=s]t₂ else [x:=s]t₃
621-
622---  ... and formally:
623-
624-section
625-set_option hygiene false in
626-local macro_rules (kind := tmBracket)
627-  | `(<{ [$x := $s] $t }>) => do
628-      `(subst $(← varStr x) <{ $s:stlcTm }> <{ $t:stlcTm }>)
629-
630-def subst (x : String) (s : Tm) (t : Tm) : Tm :=
631-  match t with
632-  -- `.var y`, not `<{ ~y }>`: `y` is the variable's *name*, a `String`
633-  -- (see the note below the definition).
634-  | .var y =>
635-      if x = y then s else t
636-  | <{ λ ~y : ~T . ~t₁ }> =>
637-      if x = y then t else <{ λ ~y : ~T . [~x := ~s] ~t₁ }>
638-  | <{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }> =>
639-      <{ ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) ([~x := ~s] ~t₂) }>
640-  | <{ true }> =>
641-      <{ true }>
642-  | <{ false }> =>
643-      <{ false }>
644-  | <{ if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }> =>
645-      <{ if [~x := ~s] ~t₁ then [~x := ~s] ~t₂ else [~x := ~s] ~t₃ }>
646-end
647-
648-macro_rules (kind := tmBracket)
649-  | `(<{ [$x := $s] $t }>) => do
650-      `(subst $(← varStr x) <{ $s:stlcTm }> <{ $t:stlcTm }>)
651-

656---  rather than as a `subst` application.

661-  match ← delabTmInner with

663-  | e => `(<{ $e:stlcTm }>)

666-
667-variable (x y : String) (s t t₁ t₂ t₃ : Tm) (T : Ty)
668-
669-@[simp] theorem subst_var_eq : <{ [~x := ~s] ~(Tm.var x) }> = s := by
670-  simp [subst]
671-
672-@[simp] theorem subst_var_ne (h : x ≠ y) : <{ [~x := ~s] ~(Tm.var y) }> = .var y := by
673-  simp [subst, h]
674-
675-@[simp] theorem subst_abs_eq : <{ [~x := ~s] (λ ~x : ~T . ~t) }> = <{ λ ~x : ~T . ~t }> := by
676-  simp [subst]
677-
678-@[simp] theorem subst_abs_ne (h : x ≠ y) :
679-    <{ [~x := ~s] (λ ~y : ~T . ~t) }> = <{ λ ~y : ~T . [~x := ~s] ~t }> := by
680-  simp [subst, h]
681-
682-@[simp] theorem subst_app :
683-    <{ [~x := ~s] (~t₁ ~t₂) }> = <{ ([~x := ~s] ~t₁) ([~x := ~s] ~t₂) }> := rfl
684-
685-@[simp] theorem subst_tru : <{ [~x := ~s] true }> = <{ true }> := rfl
686-
687-@[simp] theorem subst_fls : <{ [~x := ~s] false }> = <{ false }> := rfl
688-
689-@[simp] theorem subst_ite :
690-    <{ [~x := ~s] (if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃) }> =
691-      <{ if [~x := ~s] ~t₁ then [~x := ~s] ~t₂ else [~x := ~s] ~t₃ }> := rfl

693---  _Quiz:_
694-
695---  What is the result of the following substitution?
696-
697---    [x:=s](λy:T₁. x (λx:T₂. x))
698-
699---  (1) `(λy:T₁. x (λx:T₂. x))`
700-
701---  (2) `(λy:T₁. s (λx:T₂. s))`
702-
703---  (3) `(λy:T₁. s (λx:T₂. x))`
704-
705---  (4) none of the above
706-
707---  *Technical note*: Substitution becomes trickier to
708---  define if we consider the case where `s`, the term being
709---  substituted for a variable in some other term, may
710---  itself contain free variables. We say that `s` is an
711---  *open* term.
712-
713---  Here is an example. Using the above definition to
714---  substitute the open term
715-
716---    s = λx:Bool. r
717-
718---  (where `r` is a *free* reference to some global
719---  resource) for the free variable `z` in the term
720-
721---    t = λr:Bool. z
722-
723---  where `r` is a bound variable, we would get
724-
725---    λr:Bool. λx:Bool. r
726-
727---  where the free reference to `r` in `s` has been
728---  "captured" by the binder at the beginning of `t`.
729-
730---  Why would this be bad? Because it violates the principle
731---  that the names of bound variables do not matter. For
732---  example, if we rename the bound variable in `t`, e.g.,
733---  let
734-
735---    t' = λw:Bool. z
736-
737---  then `[z:=s]t'` is
738-
739---    λw:Bool. λx:Bool. r
740-
741---  which does not behave the same as the substituting in
742---  the original `t`:
743-
744---    [z:=s]t = λr:Bool. λx:Bool. r
745-
746---  That is, renaming a bound variable in `t` would change
747---  how `t` behaves under our simple substitution. So
748---  substitution gets more complicated in that setting, but
749---  fortunately we don't have that problem in our STLC
750---  variant.
751-
752---  Fortunately, since we are only interested here in
753---  defining the `step` relation on *closed* terms (i.e.,
754---  terms like `λx:Bool. x` that include binders for all of
755---  the variables they mention), we can sidestep this extra
756---  complexity, but it must be dealt with when formalizing
757---  richer languages.
758-
759---  ### Reduction
760-
761---  v.IsValue
762---                         -----------------------      (appAbs)
763---                          (λx:T. t) v ⟶ [x:=v]t
764-
765---                                t₁ ⟶ t₁'
766---                            ----------------          (app1)
767---                             t₁ t₂ ⟶ t₁' t₂
768-
769---                                v.IsValue
770---                                t₂ ⟶ t₂'
771---                            ----------------          (app2)
772---                             v₁ t₂ ⟶ v₁ t₂'
773-
774---  (plus the usual rules for conditionals).
775-
776---  The `appAbs` rule is often called *beta-reduction*.
777-
778---  This is *call by value* reduction: to reduce an
779---  application `(t₁ t₂)`, we
780-
781---  - first reduce `t₁` to a value: a function `λx:T. t`
782-
783---  - then reduce the argument `t₂` to a value `v`
784-
785---  - then reduce the application itself by substituting `v`
786---    for the bound variable `x` in the body `t`.
787-
788-section
789-set_option hygiene false in
790-local notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Step t t'
791-
792-inductive Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
793-  | appAbs (x : String) (T : Ty) (t v : Tm) (hv : v.IsValue) :
794-      <{ (λ ~x : ~T . ~t) ~v }> ⟶ <{ [~x := ~v] ~t }>
795-  | app1 (t₁ t₁' t₂ : Tm) (h : t₁ ⟶ t₁') :
796-      <{ ~t₁ ~t₂ }> ⟶ <{ ~t₁' ~t₂ }>
797-  | app2 (v₁ t₂ t₂' : Tm) (hv : v₁.IsValue) (h : t₂ ⟶ t₂') :
798-      <{ ~v₁ ~t₂ }> ⟶ <{ ~v₁ ~t₂' }>
799-  | ifTrue (t₁ t₂ : Tm) :
800-      <{ if true then ~t₁ else ~t₂ }> ⟶ t₁
801-  | ifFalse (t₁ t₂ : Tm) :
802-      <{ if false then ~t₁ else ~t₂ }> ⟶ t₂
803-  | ifStep (t₁ t₁' t₂ t₃ : Tm) (h : t₁ ⟶ t₁') :
804-      <{ if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }> ⟶ <{ if ~t₁' then ~t₂ else ~t₃ }>
805-end
806-
807-scoped notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Step t t'
808-scoped notation:40 t:41 " ⟶* " t':41 => Multi Step t t'

888-example : <{ ~idBB ~idB }> ⟶* idB := by
889-  apply Multi.step (y := idB)
890-  · exact .appAbs "x" <{ Bool → Bool }> <{ x }> idB idB_value
891-  · rfl

903-  -- the same reduction happens twice, so we name it
904-  have step₁ : <{ ~idBB ~idB }> ⟶ idB := by

906-  apply Multi.step (y := <{ ~idBB ~idB }>)

966---  ## Typing
967-
968---  Next we consider the typing relation of the STLC, which
969---  is meant to prevent reduction from getting stuck.
970-
971---  ### Contexts
972-
973---  *Question*: What is the type of the term "`x y`"?
974-
975---  *Answer*: It depends on the types of `x` and `y`!
976-
977---  I.e., in order to assign a type to a term, we need to
978---  know what assumptions we should make about the types of
979---  its free variables.
980-
981---  This leads us to a three-place *typing judgment*,
982---  informally written `Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T`, where `Γ` is a "typing
983---  context" — a mapping from variables to their types.
984-
985-abbrev Context := PartialMap String Ty
986-
987---  Following the usual notation for partial maps, we write
988---  `(x ↦ T, Γ)` for "update the partial function `Γ` so
989---  that it maps `x` to `T`."
990-
991---  ### Typing Relation
992-
993---  Γ x = T₁
994---                              ------------                       (var)
995---                               Γ ⊢ x ⦂ T₁
996-
997---                          x ↦ T₂ ; Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ T₁
998---                        -------------------------                (abs)
999---                         Γ ⊢ λx:T₂. t₁ ⦂ T₂ → T₁
1000-
1001---                            Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ T₂ → T₁
1002---                              Γ ⊢ t₂ ⦂ T₂
1003---                           ------------------                    (app)
1004---                             Γ ⊢ t₁ t₂ ⦂ T₁
1005-
1006---                            -----------------                    (tru)
1007---                             Γ ⊢ true ⦂ Bool
1008-
1009---                           ------------------                    (fls)
1010---                            Γ ⊢ false ⦂ Bool
1011-
1012---               Γ ⊢ t₁ ⦂ Bool    Γ ⊢ t₂ ⦂ T₁    Γ ⊢ t₃ ⦂ T₁
1013---              ---------------------------------------------      (ite)
1014---                     Γ ⊢ if t₁ then t₂ else t₃ ⦂ T₁
1015-
1016---  We can read the three-place relation `Γ ⊢ t ⦂ T` as:
1017---  "under the assumptions in Γ, the term `t` has the type
1018---  `T`."
1019-
1020---  In the formal development, we write this judgment inside
1021---  the same `<{ .. }>` brackets.
1022-
1023---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: contexts and judgments)
1024-
1025---  Contexts get a grammar of their own, `stlcCtx`. The
1026---  **meaning** is the map update we already have —
1027---  `x ↦ T ; Γ` expands to exactly the `Typeclasses`
1028---  chapter's partial-map update on `Γ` — but its surface
1029---  syntax has to be our own, because inside these brackets
1030---  all three positions are in object syntax. Writing the
1031---  map notation directly would mean writing the binding as
1032---  `"x" →ₚ <{ Bool → Bool }> ; Γ`: the name quoted, and the
1033---  type escaped back out of the brackets it belongs in. The
1034---  grammar hides those two encoding details, and nothing
1035---  else.
1036-
1037-declare_syntax_cat stlcCtx
1038-syntax:max "∅" : stlcCtx
1039-syntax:max "~" term:max : stlcCtx
1040-syntax:max stlcVar " ↦ " stlcTy " ; " stlcCtx : stlcCtx
1041-
1042-syntax:max (name := judgeBracket) "<{ " stlcCtx " ⊢ " stlcTm " ⦂ " stlcTy " }>" : term
1043-
1044-open Lean in
1045-/-- The `Context` denoted by a context expression. -/
1046-partial def ctxTerm (G : TSyntax `stlcCtx) : MacroM Term :=
1047-  match G with
1048-  | `(stlcCtx| ∅)   => `((∅ : Context))
1049-  | `(stlcCtx| ~$e) => pure e
1050-  | `(stlcCtx| $x:stlcVar ↦ $T:stlcTy ; $G:stlcCtx) => do
1051-      `(PartialMap.update $(← ctxTerm G) $(← varStr x) <{ $T:stlcTy }>)
1052-  | _ => Macro.throwUnsupported
1053-
1054---  As with `subst`, the judgment notation is used inside
1055---  the definition it names, so it is introduced in two
1056---  steps: the rule below is declared `local` with hygiene
1057---  off, so the `HasType` in its expansion resolves to the
1058---  relation being declared, and after the `section` closes
1059---  it is declared again for real use.
1060-
1061-section
1062-set_option hygiene false in
1063-local macro_rules (kind := judgeBracket)
1064-  | `(<{ $G:stlcCtx ⊢ $t:stlcTm ⦂ $T:stlcTy }>) => do
1065-      `(HasType $(← ctxTerm G) <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $T:stlcTy }>)
1066-
1067---  END DETAILS
1068-
1069-inductive HasType : Context → Tm → Ty → Prop where
1070-  | var (Γ : Context) (x : String) (T₁ : Ty) (h : Γ[x] = some T₁) :
1071-      <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~(Tm.var x) ⦂ ~T₁ }>
1072-  | abs (Γ : Context) (x : String) (T₁ T₂ : Ty) (t₁ : Tm)
1073-      (h : <{ ~x ↦ ~T₂ ; ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ ⦂ ~T₁ }>) :
1074-      <{ ~Γ ⊢ λ ~x : ~T₂ . ~t₁ ⦂ ~T₂ → ~T₁ }>
1075-  | app (Γ : Context) (T₁ T₂ : Ty) (t₁ t₂ : Tm)
1076-      (h₁ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ ⦂ ~T₂ → ~T₁ }>) (h₂ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₂ ⦂ ~T₂ }>) :
1077-      <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ ~t₂ ⦂ ~T₁ }>
1078-  | tru (Γ : Context) :
1079-      <{ ~Γ ⊢ true ⦂ Bool }>
1080-  | fls (Γ : Context) :
1081-      <{ ~Γ ⊢ false ⦂ Bool }>
1082-  | ite (Γ : Context) (t₁ t₂ t₃ : Tm) (T₁ : Ty)
1083-      (h₁ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₁ ⦂ Bool }>) (h₂ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₂ ⦂ ~T₁ }>)
1084-      (h₃ : <{ ~Γ ⊢ ~t₃ ⦂ ~T₁ }>) :
1085-      <{ ~Γ ⊢ if ~t₁ then ~t₂ else ~t₃ ⦂ ~T₁ }>
1086-
1087---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: the judgment, for real)
1088-
1089---  Closing the `section` retires the hygiene-free rule; the
1090---  same rule is then declared again, hygienically, for
1091---  every later use.
1092-
1093-end

1095-macro_rules (kind := judgeBracket)
1096-  | `(<{ $G:stlcCtx ⊢ $t:stlcTm ⦂ $T:stlcTy }>) => do
1097-      `(HasType $(← ctxTerm G) <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $T:stlcTy }>)
1098-
1099---  END DETAILS
1100-
1101---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: printing judgments back)
1102-
1103---  As with terms, a judgment prints back in its own
1104---  notation, so that a goal reads as
1105---  `<{ x ↦ Bool ; ∅ ⊢ x ⦂ Bool }>` rather than as a
1106---  `HasType` applied to a chain of map updates.
1107-
1108-open Lean PrettyPrinter in
1109-/-- Rebuild `stlcCtx` syntax from the term syntax of a `Context`, so that a
1110-context prints as `x ↦ Bool ; Γ` rather than as a chain of map updates. -/
1111-partial def unexpandCtx : Term → UnexpandM (TSyntax `stlcCtx)
1112-  | `(∅) => `(stlcCtx| ∅)
1113-  | `($x:str →ₚ $T) => do
1114-      unexpandCtx (← `($x →ₚ $T ; ∅))
1115-  | `($x:str →ₚ $T ; $G) => do
1116-      let G' ← unexpandCtx G
1117-      let x' : TSyntax `stlcVar ←
1118-        if isPlainName x.getString then
1119-          `(stlcVar| $(mkIdent (Name.mkSimple x.getString)):ident)
1120-        else `(stlcVar| ~$x)
1121-      match T with
1122-      | `(<{ $T':stlcTy }>) => `(stlcCtx| $x':stlcVar ↦ $T' ; $G')
1123-      | _                   => `(stlcCtx| $x':stlcVar ↦ ~($T) ; $G')
1124-  | G => `(stlcCtx| ~($G))
1125-
1126-open Lean PrettyPrinter in
1127-@[app_unexpander Stlc.HasType]
1128-def HasType.unexpand : Unexpander
1129-  | `($_ $G <{ $t:stlcTm }> <{ $T:stlcTy }>) =>
1130-      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ $t ⦂ $T }>)
1131-  | `($_ $G <{ $t:stlcTm }> $T) =>
1132-      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ $t ⦂ ~($T) }>)
1133-  | `($_ $G $t <{ $T:stlcTy }>) =>
1134-      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ ~($t) ⦂ $T }>)
1135-  | `($_ $G $t $T) =>
1136-      do `(<{ $(← unexpandCtx G) ⊢ ~($t) ⦂ ~($T) }>)
1137-  | _ => throw ()
1138-
1139---  END DETAILS
1140-
1141---  ### Examples
1142-
1143-example : <{ ∅ ⊢ λ x : Bool . x ⦂ Bool → Bool }> :=
1144-  .abs _ "x" _ _ _ (.var _ "x" _ rfl)
1145-
1146---  The derivation is small enough to write out directly: an
1147---  abstraction rule whose premise is the variable rule, and
1148---  the variable rule's premise — that the extended context
1149---  maps `x` to `Bool` — holds by computation, hence `rfl`.
1150-
1151---  More examples:
1152-
1153---    ∅ ⊢ λx:Bool. λy:Bool → Bool. y (y x)
1154---          ⦂ Bool → (Bool → Bool) → Bool.
1155-
1156-example :
1157-    <{ ∅ ⊢ λ x : Bool . λ y : Bool → Bool . y (y x) ⦂
1158-       Bool → (Bool → Bool) → Bool }> :=
1159-  .abs _ _ _ _ _ (.abs _ _ _ _ _
1160-    (.app _ _ Ty.bool _ _ (.var _ "y" _ rfl)
1161-      (.app _ _ Ty.bool _ _ (.var _ "y" _ rfl) (.var _ "x" _ rfl))))
1162-
1163---  We can also show that some terms are *not* typable. For
1164---  example, we can check that there is no typing derivation
1165---  assigning a type to the term `λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x y` —
1166---  i.e.,
1167-
1168---    ¬ ∃ T, ∅ ⊢ λx:Bool. λy:Bool. x y ⦂ T
1169-
1170-example : ¬ ∃ T, <{ ∅ ⊢ λ x : Bool . λ y : Bool . x y ⦂ ~T }> := by
1171-  intro ⟨T, hc⟩
1172-  -- Each `cases` peels off one rule of the derivation, naming the premise it
1173-  -- leaves behind; the context stays small because the old hypothesis goes away.
1174-  cases hc with
1175-  | abs _ _ _ _ _ h₁ =>
1176-    cases h₁ with
1177-    | abs _ _ _ _ _ h₂ =>
1178-      cases h₂ with
1179-      | app _ _ _ _ _ hf _ =>
1180-        cases hf with
1181-        | var _ _ _ hx =>
1182-          -- `x` is bound to `Bool` in the context, but the application rule
1183-          -- needs it to have an arrow type.
1184-          exact Ty.noConfusion (Option.some.inj hx)
1185-
1186---  Another nonexample:
1187-
1188---    ¬ ∃ S T, ∅ ⊢ λx:S. x x ⦂ T
1189-
1190---  _Quiz:_
1191-
1192---  Which of the following propositions is *not* provable?
1193-
1194---  (A) `y ↦ Bool ; ∅ ⊢ λx:Bool. x ⦂ Bool → Bool`
1195-
1196---  (B) `∃ T,  ∅ ⊢ λy:Bool → Bool. λx:Bool. y x ⦂ T`
1197-
1198---  (C) `∃ T,  ∅ ⊢ λy:Bool → Bool. λx:Bool. x y ⦂ T`
1199-
1200---  (D)
1201---  `∃ S, x ↦ S ; ∅ ⊢ λy:Bool → Bool. y x ⦂ (Bool → Bool) → S`
1202-
1203---  _Quiz:_
1204-
1205---  Which of these is not provable?
1206-
1207---  (A) `∃ T,  ∅ ⊢ λy:Bool → Bool → Bool. λx:Bool. y x ⦂ T`
1208-
1209---  (B) `∃ S T, x ↦ S ; ∅ ⊢ x x x ⦂ T`
1210-
1211---  (C) `∃ S U T, x ↦ S ; y ↦ U ; ∅ ⊢ λz:Bool. x (y z) ⦂ T`
1212-
1213---  (D) `∃ S T, x ↦ S ; ∅ ⊢ λy:Bool. x (x y) ⦂ T`
1214-
1215-end Stlc

TS/Types.lean

1-import Lean.PrettyPrinter.Delaborator
2-import Lean.PrettyPrinter.Parenthesizer
3-import TS.Smallstep
4-
5-import SFLCompat
6-
7---  # Types: Type Systems
8-
9---  New topic: *type systems*
10-
11---  - This chapter: a toy type system for a toy language
12-
13---    - typing relation
14---    - *progress* and *preservation* theorems
15-
16---  - Next chapter: *simply typed lambda-calculus*
17-
18---  ## Typed Arithmetic Expressions
19-
20---  - A simple toy language where expressions may fail with
21---    dynamic type errors
22-
23---    - numbers (and arithmetic)
24---    - booleans (and conditionals)
25-
26---  - This means we can write *stuck* terms like `5 + true`
27---    and `if 42 then 0 else 1`.
28-
29---  ### Syntax
30-
31---  Here is the syntax of program terms, informally:
32-
33---  t ::= true
34---      | false
35---      | if t then t else t
36---      | 0
37---      | succ t
38---      | pred t
39---      | iszero t
40-
41---  And here it is formally:
42-
43-namespace TM
44-
45-inductive Tm where
46-  | tru
47-  | fls
48-  | ite (c t e : Tm)
49-  | zero
50-  | succ (t : Tm)
51-  | pred (t : Tm)
52-  | isZero (t : Tm)
53-
54---  #### Notation
55-
56-declare_syntax_cat tm
57--- The keyword atoms (`true`/`false`/`succ`/`pred`/`iszero`) are parsed as bare
58--- identifiers and dispatched in the macro below, rather than declared as
59--- reserved symbols.  Reserving them would break ordinary Lean uses of
60--- `true`/`false` and clash with the constructor/case names `succ`, `pred`.
61-syntax:max num : tm
62-syntax:max ident : tm
63-syntax:75 ident ppHardSpace tm:76 : tm
64-syntax:max "(" tm ")" : tm
65-syntax:max "~" term:max : tm
66-syntax:50 "if " tm:51 " then " tm:51 " else " tm:51 : tm
67-syntax:max "<{ " tm " }>" : term
68-
69-open Lean in
70-macro_rules
71-  | `(<{ $n:num }>) =>
72-      if n.getNat == 0 then `(Tm.zero)
73-      else Macro.throwErrorAt n "the only numeric literal in this language is 0"
74-  | `(<{ $x:ident }>) =>
75-      match x.getId.toString with
76-      | "true"  => `(Tm.tru)
77-      | "false" => `(Tm.fls)
78-      | _ => `($x)   -- a bare identifier is a spliced Lean term (usually a variable)
79-  | `(<{ $f:ident $e:tm }>) =>
80-      match f.getId.toString with
81-      | "succ"   => `(Tm.succ <{ $e }>)
82-      | "pred"   => `(Tm.pred <{ $e }>)
83-      | "iszero" => `(Tm.isZero <{ $e }>)
84-      | _ => Macro.throwErrorAt f s!"unknown operator `{f.getId}`"
85-  | `(<{ ($e) }>) => `(<{ $e }>)
86-  | `(<{ ~$e }>)  => pure e
87-  | `(<{ if $c then $t else $e }>) => `(Tm.ite <{ $c }> <{ $t }> <{ $e }>)
88-
89---  THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED (Notation encoding: printing terms back)
90-
91-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Parenthesizer in
92-/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `tm` output according to the grammar's precedences. -/
93-@[category_parenthesizer tm]
94-def tm.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
95-  maybeParenthesize `tm true wrapParens prec <|
96-    parenthesizeCategoryCore `tm prec
97-where
98-  wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
99-    let pstx ← `(tm| ($(⟨stx⟩)))
100-    return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
101-
102-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
103-/-- Rebuild `tm` concrete syntax from a `Tm` term. -/
104-partial def delabTmInner : DelabM (TSyntax `tm) := do
105-  let stx ←
106-    match_expr ← getExpr with
107-    | Tm.tru => `(tm| $(mkIdent `true):ident)
108-    | Tm.fls => `(tm| $(mkIdent `false):ident)
109-    | Tm.zero => `(tm| 0)
110-    | Tm.succ _ => do `(tm| $(mkIdent `succ):ident $(← withAppArg delabTmInner))
111-    | Tm.pred _ => do `(tm| $(mkIdent `pred):ident $(← withAppArg delabTmInner))
112-    | Tm.isZero _ => do `(tm| $(mkIdent `iszero):ident $(← withAppArg delabTmInner))
113-    | Tm.ite _ _ _ => do
114-        let c ← withAppFn <| withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
115-        let t ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabTmInner
116-        let e ← withAppArg delabTmInner
117-        `(tm| if $c then $t else $e)
118-    | _ => do
119-        -- A bare variable prints without the `~` escape; anything else keeps it.
120-        match ← delab with
121-        | `($i:ident) => `(tm| $i:ident)
122-        | e => `(tm| ~$e)
123-  (⟨·⟩) <$> annotateTermInfo ⟨stx.raw⟩
124-
125-open Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr in
126--- The keys are the constants' full names: `Tm` lives in namespace `TM`, and the
127--- `delab` attribute does not resolve its argument against the current namespace.
128-@[delab app.TM.Tm.tru, delab app.TM.Tm.fls, delab app.TM.Tm.zero, delab app.TM.Tm.succ,
129-  delab app.TM.Tm.pred, delab app.TM.Tm.isZero, delab app.TM.Tm.ite]
130-partial def delabTm : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
131-  guard <| match_expr ← getExpr with
132-    | Tm.tru => true | Tm.fls => true | Tm.zero => true
133-    | Tm.succ _ => true | Tm.pred _ => true | Tm.isZero _ => true
134-    | Tm.ite _ _ _ => true | _ => false
135-  match ← delabTmInner with
136-  | `(tm| ~$e) => pure e
137-  | e => `(<{ $e }>)
138-
139---  END DETAILS
140-
141---  #### Values
142-
143---  *Values* are `true`, `false`, and numeric values (`0`,
144---  and `succ` of a numeric value).
145-
146-inductive Tm.IsBValue : Tm → Prop where
147-  | tru : Tm.IsBValue <{ true }>
148-  | fls : Tm.IsBValue <{ false }>
149-
150-inductive Tm.IsNValue : Tm → Prop where
151-  | zero : Tm.IsNValue <{ 0 }>
152-  | succ (t : Tm) (h : Tm.IsNValue t) : Tm.IsNValue <{ succ t }>
153-
154-def Tm.IsValue (t : Tm) : Prop := Tm.IsBValue t ∨ Tm.IsNValue t
155-
156---  ### Operational Semantics
157-
158---  -----------------------------                 (ifTrue)
159---                     if true then t1 else t2 ⟶ t1
160-
161---                     ------------------------------                (ifFalse)
162---                     if false then t1 else t2 ⟶ t2
163-
164---                                t1 ⟶ t1'
165---              -----------------------------------------------      (ifStep)
166---              if t1 then t2 else t3 ⟶ if t1' then t2 else t3
167-
168---                                t1 ⟶ t1'
169---                           -------------------                     (succStep)
170---                           succ t1 ⟶ succ t1'
171-
172---                             -----------                           (predZero)
173---                             pred 0 ⟶ 0
174-
175---                              IsNValue v
176---                          ------------------                       (predSucc)
177---                          pred (succ v) ⟶ v
178-
179---                                t1 ⟶ t1'
180---                           -------------------                     (predStep)
181---                           pred t1 ⟶ pred t1'
182-
183---                            ----------------                       (isZeroZero)
184---                            iszero 0 ⟶ true
185-
186---                               IsNValue v
187---                        ------------------------                   (isZeroSucc)
188---                        iszero (succ v) ⟶ false
189-
190---                                t1 ⟶ t1'
191---                         -----------------------                   (isZeroStep)
192---                         iszero t1 ⟶ iszero t1'
193-
194-section
195-set_option hygiene false in
196-local notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Tm.Step t t'
197-inductive Tm.Step : Tm → Tm → Prop where
198-  | ifTrue (t1 t2 : Tm) : <{ if true then t1 else t2 }> ⟶ t1
199-  | ifFalse (t1 t2 : Tm) : <{ if false then t1 else t2 }> ⟶ t2
200-  | ifStep (c c' t2 t3 : Tm) (h : c ⟶ c') :
201-      <{ if c then t2 else t3 }> ⟶ <{ if c' then t2 else t3 }>
202-  | succStep (t1 t1' : Tm) (h : t1 ⟶ t1') : <{ succ t1 }> ⟶ <{ succ t1' }>
203-  | predZero : <{ pred 0 }> ⟶ <{ 0 }>
204-  | predSucc (v : Tm) (hv : Tm.IsNValue v) : <{ pred (succ v) }> ⟶ v
205-  | predStep (t1 t1' : Tm) (h : t1 ⟶ t1') : <{ pred t1 }> ⟶ <{ pred t1' }>
206-  | isZeroZero : <{ iszero 0 }> ⟶ <{ true }>
207-  | isZeroSucc (v : Tm) (hv : Tm.IsNValue v) : <{ iszero (succ v) }> ⟶ <{ false }>
208-  | isZeroStep (t1 t1' : Tm) (h : t1 ⟶ t1') : <{ iszero t1 }> ⟶ <{ iszero t1' }>
209-end
210-
211-scoped notation:40 t:41 " ⟶ " t':41 => Tm.Step t t'
212-
213---  ### Normal Forms and Values
214-
215---  The first interesting thing to notice about this
216---  `Tm.Step` relation is that the strong progress theorem
217---  from the Smallstep chapter fails here. That is, there
218---  are terms that are normal forms (they can't take a step)
219---  but not values (they are not included in our definition
220---  of possible "results of reduction").
221-
222---  Such terms are *stuck*.
223-
224-def Tm.IsNormalForm (t : Tm) : Prop := _root_.IsNormalForm Tm.Step t
225-
226-def Tm.IsStuck (t : Tm) : Prop := Tm.IsNormalForm t ∧ ¬ Tm.IsValue t
227-
228---  ### Exercise (2 stars): some_term_is_stuck ⭐⭐
229-
230-theorem some_term_is_stuck : ∃ t, Tm.IsStuck t := by
231-  sorry
232-
233---  However, although values and normal forms are *not* the
234---  same in this language, the set of values is a subset of
235---  the set of normal forms.
236-
237---  This is important because it shows we did not
238---  accidentally define things so that some value could
239---  still take a step.
240-
241-theorem nvalue_is_nf (t : Tm) (h : Tm.IsNValue t) : Tm.IsNormalForm t := by
242-  induction h with
243-  | zero => intro hc; obtain ⟨t', hstp⟩ := hc; cases hstp
244-  | succ t0 hn0 ih =>
245-      intro hc; obtain ⟨t', hstp⟩ := hc
246-      cases hstp with
247-      | succStep _ t1' h => exact ih ⟨t1', h⟩
248-
249---  ### Exercise (3 stars): value_is_nf ⭐⭐⭐
250-
251---  (Hint: You will reach a point in this proof where you
252---  need to use an induction to reason about a term that is
253---  known to be a numeric value. This induction can be
254---  performed either over the term itself or over the
255---  evidence that it is a numeric value. The proof goes
256---  through in either case, but you will find that one way
257---  is quite a bit shorter than the other. For the sake of
258---  the exercise, try to complete the proof both ways.)
259-
260-theorem value_is_nf (t : Tm) (h : Tm.IsValue t) : Tm.IsNormalForm t := by
261-  sorry
262-
263---  The "other way" mentioned in the hint proves the same
264---  fact by induction on the term itself rather than on the
265---  evidence that it is a numeric value. It goes through,
266---  but is a bit longer than the `nvalue_is_nf` route above.
267-
268-theorem value_is_nf' : ∀ t, Tm.IsValue t → Tm.IsNormalForm t := by
269-  sorry
270-
271---  ### Exercise (3 stars): step_deterministic (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐
272-
273---  Use `value_is_nf` (here, `nvalue_is_nf`) to show that
274---  the `Tm.Step` relation is also deterministic.
275-
276-theorem step_deterministic : Deterministic Tm.Step := by
277-  sorry

279---  _Quiz:_
280-
281---  Is the following term stuck?
282-
283---  iszero (if true then (succ 0) else 0)
284-
285---  (A) Yes (B) No
286-
287---  _Quiz:_
288-
289---  What about this one? Is it stuck?
290-
291---  if (succ 0) then true else false
292-
293---  (A) Yes (B) No
294-
295---  _Quiz:_
296-
297---  What about this one? Is it stuck?
298-
299---  succ (succ 0)
300-
301---  (A) Yes (B) No

308-

310-
311---  (Hint: Notice that the `Tm.Step` relation doesn't care
312---  about whether the expression being stepped makes global
313---  sense — it just checks that the operation in the *next*
314---  reduction step is being applied to the right kinds of
315---  operands.)
316-
317---  Suppose we define an alternate single-step relation,
318---  written `t ⇢ t'`, that *drops* the `Tm.IsNValue` premise
319---  from the `predSucc` and `isZeroSucc` rules — so
320---  `pred (succ t)` and `iszero (succ t)` may step even when
321---  `t` is not a numeric value. (It is built with exactly
322---  the same notation setup as `Tm.Step`; note
323---  `predSucc`/`isZeroSucc` no longer take a premise.)
324-
325-section
326-set_option hygiene false in
327-local notation:40 t:41 " ⇢ " t':41 => Tm.AltStep t t'
328-inductive Tm.AltStep : Tm → Tm → Prop where
329-  | ifTrue (t1 t2 : Tm) : <{ if true then t1 else t2 }> ⇢ t1
330-  | ifFalse (t1 t2 : Tm) : <{ if false then t1 else t2 }> ⇢ t2
331-  | ifStep (t1 t1' t2 t3 : Tm) : t1 ⇢ t1' →
332-      <{ if t1 then t2 else t3 }> ⇢ <{ if t1' then t2 else t3 }>
333-  | succStep (t1 t1' : Tm) : t1 ⇢ t1' → <{ succ t1 }> ⇢ <{ succ t1' }>
334-  | predZero : <{ pred 0 }> ⇢ <{ 0 }>
335-  | predSucc (t1 : Tm) : <{ pred (succ t1) }> ⇢ t1
336-  | predStep (t1 t1' : Tm) : t1 ⇢ t1' → <{ pred t1 }> ⇢ <{ pred t1' }>
337-  | isZeroZero : <{ iszero 0 }> ⇢ <{ true }>
338-  | isZeroSucc (t1 : Tm) : <{ iszero (succ t1) }> ⇢ <{ false }>
339-  | isZeroStep (t1 t1' : Tm) : t1 ⇢ t1' → <{ iszero t1 }> ⇢ <{ iszero t1' }>
340-end
341-
342-scoped notation:40 t:41 " ⇢ " t':41 => Tm.AltStep t t'
343-
344---  Some questions about this relation (answers inline):
345-
346---  - Is `⇢` deterministic
347---    (`∀ t t' t'', t ⇢ t' → t ⇢ t'' → t' = t''`)? No:
348---    `pred (succ (pred 0))` steps to both `pred 0` (by
349---    `predSucc`) and `pred (succ 0)` (by `predStep`, since
350---    `pred 0 ⇢ 0`).
351-
352---  - Is every `Tm.Step` normal form also a `⇢` normal form?
353---    No: `pred (succ true)` is stuck for `Tm.Step` but
354---    steps under `⇢` (to `true`, by `predSucc`, now that
355---    the `Tm.IsNValue` premise is gone).
356-
357---  - Is every `⇢` normal form also a `Tm.Step` normal form?
358---    Yes — `Tm.Step` is a subrelation of `⇢`, so anything
359---    stuck for `⇢` is stuck for `Tm.Step`.
360-
361---  - Is every value reachable by `Tm.Step` (in many steps)
362---    also reachable by `⇢` (in many steps)? Yes, for the
363---    same subrelation reason.
364-
365---  - Conversely? No: `iszero (succ true)` reaches the value
366---    `false` under `⇢` but is stuck under `Tm.Step`.
367-
368---  A *functional* version computes a single `⇢` step of a
369---  term, returning `none` when the term is a `⇢` normal
370---  form. This is a nice chance to see a step *function*,
371---  which the chapter otherwise gives only as a relation:
372-
373-def alt_simplify_step (t : Tm) : Option Tm :=
374-  match t with
375-  | <{ if t1 then t2 else t3 }> =>
376-      match alt_simplify_step t1 with
377-      | some t1' => some <{ if t1' then t2 else t3 }>
378-      | none =>
379-        match t1 with
380-        | <{ true }>  => some t2
381-        | <{ false }> => some t3
382-        | _           => none
383-  | <{ succ t1 }> =>
384-      match alt_simplify_step t1 with
385-      | some t1' => some <{ succ t1' }>
386-      | none     => none
387-  | <{ pred t1 }> =>
388-      match alt_simplify_step t1 with

493---  ### Canonical forms
494-
495---  The following two lemmas capture the fundamental fact
496---  that the definitions of boolean and numeric values agree
497---  with the typing relation: a well-typed value of type
498---  `Bool` is a boolean value, and of type `Nat` a numeric
499---  value.
500-
501-theorem bool_canonical (t : Tm) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ Bool }>) (hv : Tm.IsValue t) : Tm.IsBValue t := by
502-  cases hv with
503-  | inl hb => exact hb
504-  | inr hn => cases hn with
505-    | zero => cases hT
506-    | succ t0 h => cases hT
507-
508-theorem nat_canonical (t : Tm) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ Nat }>) (hv : Tm.IsValue t) : Tm.IsNValue t := by
509-  cases hv with
510-  | inl hb => cases hb <;> cases hT
511-  | inr hn => exact hn

513---  ### Progress
514-
515---  The typing relation enjoys two critical properties.
516-
517---  The first is that well-typed normal forms are not stuck
518---  — or conversely, if a term is well typed, then either it
519---  is a value or it can take at least one step. We call
520---  this *progress*.
521-

529-theorem progress (t : Tm) (T : Ty) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>) : Tm.IsValue t ∨ ∃ t', t ⟶ t' := by

548---  ### Exercise (3 stars): finish_progress_informal (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐
549-
550---  Complete the corresponding informal proof.
551-
552---  *Theorem*: If `⊢ t ⦂ T`, then either `t` is a value or
553---  else `t ⟶ t'` for some `t'`.
554-
555---  *Proof*: By induction on a derivation of `⊢ t ⦂ T`.
556-
557---  - If the last rule in the derivation is `ite`, then
558---    `t = if t1 then t2
559---        else t3`, with `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool`,
560---    `⊢ t2 ⦂ T` and `⊢ t3 ⦂ T`. By the IH, either `t1` is a
561---    value or else `t1` can step to some `t1'`.
562-
563---    - If `t1` is a value, then by the canonical forms
564---      lemmas and the fact that `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool` we have that
565---      `t1` is a boolean value (`Tm.IsBValue`) — i.e., it
566---      is either `true` or `false`. If `t1 = true`, then
567---      `t` steps to `t2` by `ifTrue`, while if
568---      `t1 = false`, then `t` steps to `t3` by `ifFalse`.
569---      Either way, `t` can step, which is what we wanted to
570---      show.
571-
572---    - If `t1` itself can take a step, then, by `ifStep`,
573---      so can `t`.

610---  ### Type Preservation
611-
612---  The second critical property of typing is that, when a
613---  well-typed term takes a step, the result is a well-typed
614---  term (of the same type).
615-

619---  property. (Again, make sure you understand the informal

622-theorem preservation (t t' : Tm) (T : Ty) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>) (he : t ⟶ t') : <{ ⊢ t' ⦂ T }> := by

625---  ### Exercise (3 stars): finish_preservation_informal (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐
626-
627---  Complete the following informal proof.
628-
629---  *Theorem*: If `⊢ t ⦂ T` and `t ⟶ t'`, then `⊢ t' ⦂ T`.
630-
631---  *Proof*: By induction on a derivation of `⊢ t ⦂ T`.
632-
633---  - If the last rule in the derivation is `ite`, then
634---    `t = if t1 then t2
635---        else t3`, with `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool`,
636---    `⊢ t2 ⦂ T` and `⊢ t3 ⦂ T`.
637-
638---    Inspecting the rules for the small-step reduction
639---    relation and remembering that `t` has the form
640---    `if ...`, we see that the only ones that could have
641---    been used to prove `t ⟶ t'` are `ifTrue`, `ifFalse`,
642---    or `ifStep`.
643-
644---    - If the last rule was `ifTrue`, then `t' = t2`. But
645---      we know that `⊢ t2 ⦂ T`, so we are done.
646-
647---    - If the last rule was `ifFalse`, then `t' = t3`. But
648---      we know that `⊢ t3 ⦂ T`, so we are done.
649-
650---    - If the last rule was `ifStep`, then
651---      `t' = if t1' then t2 else t3`, where `t1 ⟶ t1'`. We
652---      know `⊢ t1 ⦂ Bool` so, by the IH,
653---      `⊢ t1' ⦂
654---            Bool`. The `ite` rule then gives us
655---      `⊢ if t1' then t2 else t3 ⦂ T`, as required.

669---  ### Type Soundness
670-
671---  Putting progress and preservation together, we see that
672---  a well-typed term can never reach a stuck state.
673-
674-def Tm.MultiStep (t1 t2 : Tm) : Prop := Multi Tm.Step t1 t2
675-
676-scoped notation:40 t1:41 " ⟶* " t2:41 => Tm.MultiStep t1 t2
677-
678-theorem soundness (t t' : Tm) (T : Ty) (hT : <{ ⊢ t ⦂ T }>) (hm : t ⟶* t') : ¬ Tm.IsStuck t' := by
679-  induction hm generalizing T with
680-  | refl a =>
681-      intro hst; obtain ⟨hnf, hnv⟩ := hst
682-      cases progress a T hT with
683-      | inl hv => exact hnv hv
684-      | inr hs => exact hnf hs
685-  | step a b c h1 h2 ih => exact ih T (preservation a b T hT h1)
